speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF UNION WITH DOMINION OF CANADA, MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a matter of special privilege and of interest, I am sure, to all hon. members of the house, may I take a moment to refer to the event of which the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) reminded the house yesterday. Even if he had not done so I am sure hon. members would have felt that today should not pass without our recalling that at midnight tonight Newfoundland will have been a Canadian province for a full year. It seems to me that, without any formal motion, the house would like to extend to tha people of our tenth province greetings and good wishes on this occasion. We have all been delighted at the way in which hon. members from Newfoundland on both sides have contributed to our proceedings. They are at home with the rest of us, and we are at home with them. That, I believe, is the spirit in which Newfoundland has fitted, and will continue to fit, into our Canadian union.

speakeroldname: Hon. F. G. Bradley (Secretary of State):
subtopic: FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF UNION WITH DOMINION OF CANADA, MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the 31st day of March, and in a few hours we shall stand on the threshold of Newfoundland's second year as a province of Canada. It may not be inappropriate that at this time I should make brief reference to our first year of partnership with the other provinces of our nation. I want to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the words which have just fallen from his lips. They constitute an official confirmation of the fact that the other provinces of Canada and its citizens from east to west have received our people and our country as one of themselves.
From 1933 until 1946 Newfoundland experienced what some people were pleased to term a holiday from politics. In the latter year began a period of political warfare of various types which continued unceasingly until June of 1949. We had a national convention election, with all the guerrilla warfare and pitched battles which followed in its wake. We had the campaigns of two referenda. We had a provincial election, and, lastly, a federal election in June last. The net result of these three years of uninterrupted political battle was that we became the
tenth province of the nation, with Liberal ministries returned to power in both federal and provincial fields.
To date, our experience of provincehood has been a short one-too short to measure long-term results with any degree of accuracy. But we can perhaps estimate broadly the prospects for the future, even by the short experience of the last twelve months.
The reception which was accorded to my countrymen and myself upon our first appearance in this honourable assembly of the Commons of Canada was so spontaneous and wholehearted that even the most implacable and irreconcilable anti-confederationist must have been convinced that our position here was not that of unwelcome guests, but that of valued members of the Canadian family of free people extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
During the year, changing world conditions indicated that difficulties lay ahead in many of our foreign markets, and there were indications that our favourable position as sellers, which had continued for a number of years, was disappearing. Outlets for pit props, pulp-wood and sulphite practically dried up, with the resultant substantial unemployment in the industries concerned, as well as in certain other fields which ordinarily profit by their activity. In some sections of the country a short fishery added to our difficulties. In these circumstances the value of Canadian social services in the fields of unemployment insurance, family allowances, and indirectly even old age pensions, has been very substantial, and their beneficial effects are apparent even to the most casual observer.
The prospective problems which our people now face as a result of increased competition from soft currency countries, the devaluation of the pound, and the difficulty of obtaining convertible currency for sales in our European market, are of a character which might prove almost beyond the powers of an independent Newfoundland. Our people are heartened by the knowledge that their negligible bargaining power in the world markets is now supplemented by the weight and influence of this nation.
In the field of modernization of our basic industries there is much to be done. Aids to navigation and the industries of the sea, which are essential to any program in this field, are already under way and in contemplation.

Newfoundland
Extensive research, aimed at increased production at lower costs, is to commence this year and will, I believe, in the foreseeable future, bring revolutionary economic improvement in this ancient and pre-eminently important Newfoundland industry.
Union has inevitably brought some stresses and strains. No reform was ever effected painlessly, but I am quite sure that the net effects thus far have been of great benefit to our people. And the unquestionable desire of the federal government to aid necessary development in every possible way gives confidence in the future, and an assurance that A'e made no mistake in joining the great Canadian family.
I have been a confederationist for nearly forty years. Our struggle to achieve union covered a period of three years of intensive effort against the honest, though mistaken, views of many opponents, and ended in victory but twelve short months ago. The experience of the year which is just expiring has proven to me that, amongst any achievements in my lifetime which may be laid to my credit, my share in bringing about this union stands pre-eminent. In the light of the events of the last twelve months, I am further assured that it is the effort in my career in which I can take the greatest pride.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
subtopic: FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF UNION WITH DOMINION OF CANADA, MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself and the members of my party with the expression of good wishes that has been conveyed in this house to Newfoundland on the first anniversary of its becoming a member of this great partnership. I should think that on this occasion every Canadian would wish to extend to the people of Newfoundland the simple but well-understood greeting, "Many happy returns of the day".
We now share with the people of Newfoundland that justifiable feeling of pride which has been earned through centuries of effort and fortitude by the sturdy people who inhabit the oldest British colony in North America. Today one can still see there the souvenirs of these earliest settlements which really laid the foundation for the establishment of our system of free democracy on the North American continent.
Newfoundland, by its geographical position, was from the early days the bulwark of this settlement which gradually spread over the whole of North America. Much has happened since those early days when John Cabot, and others following after him, discovered the great possibilities of that rugged, challenging, and beautiful island. We have passed from the time of the small sailing ships to the present period of extremely fast transportation which now brings Newfoundland within

a few hours of Great Britain and the European continent. It is in that modern world that the adjustments which are inevitable with a new association of this kind must be made. These developments of the past few years offer new opportunities to the people of Newfoundland, as they do to the rest of Canada. As a result of this union I would hope that vast new opportunities will open up for the people of that province, through the employment of their water power and other natural resources.
This marriage between Newfoundland and Canada, like even the happiest marriages, is not without some difficult adjustments. I feel certain that all Canadians who have welcomed Newfoundland so wholeheartedly into this union will express the hope that everything may be done by the government of Canada and the people of Canada to make the people of Newfoundland increasingly happy in this new association.

subtopic: FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF UNION WITH DOMINION OF CANADA, MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
Although my remarks will not be lengthy, Mr. Speaker, they will be none the less sincere. May I say that we join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and all other members of the house in expressing our appreciation that at last confederation has been consummated. We hope and believe that the first year of this association has been a happy one, and we feel sure that it augurs well for the future.
The Secretary of State referred to the bitter controversy that occurred in Newfoundland prior to confederation. I was glad yesterday when the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) rose in his place, expressed his appreciation of the union, and introduced no note of partisanship. That, after all, Mr. Speaker, is the manner in which this house carried on the discussions which led to confederation. Differences of opinion there were with regard to details, but it is a happy instance of good will that, in reference to this parliament at least, there was unanimity in welcoming Newfoundland into confederation.

subtopic: FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF UNION WITH DOMINION OF CANADA, MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
I think it is fitting, Mr. Speaker, that this house should mark the end of the first year of Newfoundland's membership in the Canadian family of provinces and the beginning of their second year. At this moment I do not wish to do more than to join with those who have spoken in wishing the people of Newfoundland well, and to say to them that it has only been about forty-five years since Alberta joined the confederation. We have had our ups and downs; we have had to kick a time or two about the

way things were going; but, all in all, we have been happy that we came in. I am sure that the people of Newfoundland, at the end of their forty-five years, will feel the same way.
Judging from the calibre of the members of this house sent to us by Newfoundland, I would say that the people in Newfoundland in the future will be happy and will be one with us. I think we all feel much like the parents who have finally seen the last member of the family in at night and safely in bed.

subtopic: FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF UNION WITH DOMINION OF CANADA, MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been my happy experience during the last three decades to have associated with me two gentlemen from Newfoundland and their families. The Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) spoke about some basic industry in Newfoundland. I just could not hear what he said, but I thought to myself that perhaps the greatest basic industry of the people there is to produce fine citizens, some of whom come and settle in other parts of Canada.
I want to take this opportunity of mentioning two names. One of them is Eli Frank Benson, a former neighbour of mine, whose dear wife is still alive, although he has passed on; she was the daughter of a Methodist minister. The family are still neighbours of mine. He had been associated with me for some twenty-five years, and did a great deal to help build up the industry of Canada. The other one is Stanley Patrick Martin, also of Newfoundland, whose widow and family are still in my community. These were two men from Newfoundland with whom it was my privilege to be associated. In common with thousands of others they did a great deal to help build up Canada.
I hope that the basic industry to which I referred will continue to produce such men. I am happy to have this opportunity of being associated more and more closely with the province in which is included the constituency of the Secretary of State.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the privilege of being allowed to pay tribute to these two families.

speechtext:
May I direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries, notice

Inquiries of the Ministry of which I have sent him? Has the minister recently signed a treaty or convention with the United States government with respect to halibut fishing on the Pacific coast? If so, will the minister make a statement as to the provisions of that treaty, and whether it will extend or split the halibut season?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
subsubtopic: RECIPROCAL PORT PRIVILEGES TO CANADIAN AND U.S. FISHERMEN
speechtext:
The convention signed last week with the United States is not a revision of the existing Pacific halibut fishery convention. The new convention gives to United States and Canadian halibut fishermen reciprocal port privileges on the Pacific coast. These privileges allow Canadian fishermen to land their catches of halibut and sablefish in Alaska or other United States ports, to sell them locally on payment of duty, or transport them in bond to any part of either country. Our fishermen are allowed entry into United States ports also to obtain supplies, repairs and equipment. Similar concessions are granted to the United States halibut fleet in British Columbia ports.
Formerly the two governments had to pass enabling legislation each year to make this possible. The new convention will permit the continuous exchange of these privileges. In addition, the new convention gives Canadian halibut vessels these rights in ports of the United States proper as well as of Alaska. It has nothing to do with a split season.

subsubtopic: RECIPROCAL PORT PRIVILEGES TO CANADIAN AND U.S. FISHERMEN
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? Is there not a treaty being negotiated between Canada and the United States which will deal with the halibut season and other related matters? If so, when is it expected that the treaty will be concluded?

subsubtopic: RECIPROCAL PORT PRIVILEGES TO CANADIAN AND U.S. FISHERMEN
speechtext: There was a meeting of the halibut commission last fall in Prince Rupert, and also in Alaska. This matter was then discussed, but no agreement was reached. There will be another meeting of the halibut commission shortly, and they may decide then to split the season, or they may not. However, it will be decided by the commission.

subsubtopic: RECIPROCAL PORT PRIVILEGES TO CANADIAN AND U.S. FISHERMEN
speechtext: There is no new treaty being negotiated?

subsubtopic: RECIPROCAL PORT PRIVILEGES TO CANADIAN AND U.S. FISHERMEN

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Yes. Perhaps in introducing these estimates, Mr. Chairman, I should make a statement. In doing so it will be my purpose to review briefly the trading position of the past year, 1949, and to give an analysis of prospects for the year 1950 as they are seen by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
A discussion of trade cannot be wholly separated from a discussion of the economic position of Canada. But as a good deal has been said about our economic position, particularly by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech and in earlier speeches, I will touch on the economy of the country only to the extent necessary to explain the trade position.
I need not tell hon. members that the past year has been one of extreme and violent world changes and adjustments. We have seen nations disappear behind the iron curtain. An example is the great nation of China, which was an important customer and supplier of Canada. Other nations have had changes of government which have not been to the benefit of Canadian trade. The shortage of dollars has caused the employment of restrictive practices, the result being prohibitions, quotas, and various arbitrary methods of cutting down dollar expenditures. We have been faced with a lack of convertibility of currencies, and this today is one of the serious obstacles to a free exchange of goods.
Another consideration has been the shift of economic power from Europe to North America, which has been important in dictating the conditions of movement of trade between North America and other countries. However, in spite of all these difficulties, the past year has been a prosperous one. Our economy has been riding pretty well on the crest of the wave. We can look back to 1949 as a very prosperous year for Canada.
I think it is remarkable that while other countries have been experiencing social and economic upheavals incidental to post-war . readjustment, Canada has been almost totally unscathed during the reconversion period. I think it is too much to hope that we can complete our own adjustment fully without receiving a few scars, but up to the moment I think we can count ourselves as the most fortunate 55946-92
Supply-Trade and Commerce nation on earth in having escaped any serious difficulties in bringing about the adjustment from war to peace.
In discussing the future situation it is my purpose to give a fair balance as between the favourable factors and the unfavourable factors. As the Irish might put it, I intend to give a balanced statement, with the weight of the balance on the side of the unfavourable factor. I am not pessimistic about the future, but, as always, I shall try to give the committee my own outlook, and the reasons for it, without introducing undue optimism into the statement.
Let me give first a summary of trade for 1949. The exports for that year were very close to the peacetime high. As a matter of fact there was a drop in exports amounting to about three per cent of our total. Imports were about the same as in the previous year. We had a favourable balance of trade of about $250 million during 1949.
It is more and more the tendency, in discussing Canada's external trade, to discuss it in separate compartments. Perhaps I might first discuss our trade with the United States. That trade last year amounted to about $3,500 million, which is by far the largest trade between any two other countries in the world. As a matter of fact it is larger than the trade of the United States with any other four countries in the world.
Our exports to the United States last year were about the same as in the previous year, standing at about $1,500 million. Our imports from the United States increased by about $160 million. One contributing factor to that -and there are several-was the relaxation of restrictions that had been put on when we found it necessary to correct our dollar exchange position. But a very important contributing factor was the recession of business in the United States, which occurred about the middle of that year. Many items which up to that time had been in short supply became available from the United States in ample supply; as Canada was carrying out a very large investment program, a good many orders that had been placed previously were shipped in over the period of two or three months, and a great increase in our trade for those months appears in the statistics.
As I have said, however, we sold to the United States last year $1,524 million worth of goods, and we bought from that country $1,952 million worth of goods. In other words, we sent to the United States about fifty per cent of our exports, and bought from the United States about seventy per cent of our imports.
The balance of payments position on account of the larger imports without an

Supply-Trade and Commerce increase in exports worsened by about $200 million, to which dividend payments' from Canada contributed. So that our balance of payments position with the United States was about $200 million worse for 1949 than it had been for 1948. In other words, our adverse balance of payments position rose from about $400 million in 1948 to $600 million in 1949.
When we turn to the balance of our trade with the rest of the world we find the position reversed. Instead of being on the same side as our overseas customers vis-a-vis the United States, we find that in our overseas trade we are on the same side as the United States vis-a-vis most of the world.
Taking, for simplicity, our total merchandise trade exclusive of the United States, we had in 1949 an export surplus of $690 million and a current balance-of-payments credit of some $800 million. About fifteen per cent of our overseas trade was with the dollar countries of Latin America. That presented no dollar problem. But for the balance of our trade we had to meet the difficulty of selling in dollars as against other countries selling in sterling. The fact that we were able to maintain our position in overseas markets is, I suggest, rather remarkable, taking into account all the unfavourable circumstances that faced our trade in those markets.
When we turn to the United Kingdom we find that our exports to that country actually rose $20 million above the level of 1948. The year 1949 was in fact the year of greatest exports to the United Kingdom of any peacetime year in history. I call that particularly to the attention of the committee, because, from statements which have been made during the past year in the house, one would almost assume that our market in the United Kingdom was gone forever. The fact of the matter is that our exports to England actually increased during last year.
Our total overseas exports, however, fell by some $90 million, or less than six per cent of our overseas trade. The reason for that was that some of our trade in the previous year had been unusual, in that it had included replacement of capital equipment. There were large items such as locomotives and railway rolling stock shipped to India, Egypt and South Africa. There was the sale of ships to overseas buyers. Those unusual items more than account for the drop in trade. Had these capital replacement items been cancelled out, our exports to overseas markets would have been about the same as in the previous year.
Our imports from the United Kingdom were slightly higher than in the previous year. Determined efforts are being made to step up
tMr. Howe.]
imports from the United Kingdom, but the program is necessarily long-range, and we expect much more decided improvement in that direction during 1950 than we were able to achieve in 1949.
To sum up our trade picture in two sentences, in 1949 our exports to the United States were maintained in spite of a recession there, while our imports were increased, largely for productive and new investment purposes. Our overseas exports fell about six per cent, and while there was an increase in imports from the United Kingdom, there was a small over-all decline in total imports from overseas countries. Our adverse balance of trade with the United States consequently increased significantly, while our large favourable balance with the rest of the world was slightly reduced.
Turning now to 1950, we expect that our exports to the United States will rise substantially, and we expect our imports from that country to fall. The trade returns for the first and second months of this year support that view. In January and February our exports to the United States were up $38 million and our imports were down $15 million, improving our trade balance with the United States by $53 million. We regard that as a trend likely to continue throughout the year, for various reasons which I need not go into, one of which is the increased production of exportable commodities in Canada, such as petroleum and iron ore.
We expect some drop in our exports to the United Kingdom and to the rest of the world. We have not been able to measure the extent of the drop. In the first two months of the year there was a drop in exports to England of $20 million, but it is not definite at the moment whether that fairly indicates the trend. The drop of $20 million in January and February was accounted for almost entirely by lower shipments of wheat. The reason shipments of wheat were lower was that we found it impossible to deliver wheat in sufficient quantity at the seaboard to meet commitments and had to ask the government of the United Kingdom to permit us to postpone shipments of a substantial amount of wheat. That wheat will come back into the trade figures in April and May, and I am not sure that the drop of $20 million in January and February is particularly significant.
We know that the government of the United Kingdom has in hand a belt-tightening _ program designed to save dollars and we are pretty certain to feel the effect of that program over the new year. On the other hand we believe that there will be an increase in imports from the United Kingdom as a result

of the current dollar-sterling effort and in consequence of efforts that have been made already.
So far as the rest of the world is concerned, the situation in Argentina is disturbing to the point where we have been able to trade very little. Dollar markets have been practically closed in that country. Trade with the rest * of South America continues on a fairly stable basis, and the probabilities are that exports to overseas countries, excluding the United Kingdom and the sterling area generally, will be on about the same level as those of the past year.
During the past year we took in various trade discussions, including the tripartite talks in Washington having to do with trade between the United Kingdom and the sterling area generally, the United States and Canada. We will also take part in another trade discussion at Torquay to follow up the trade discussions at Geneva and Annecy. It is well to keep in mind that the trade discussions at Geneva played a great part in opening up markets in the United States and making possible the considerable increase of exports to that country. Some forty nations will meet at Torquay in September of this year, and we hope that meeting will result in a still further lowering of trade barriers between participating nations.
As a trade promotional effort I may mention the international trade fair to be held once again in Canada at the end of May. This trade fair has been most helpful, particularly to our overseas customers in opening up Canadian markets for their goods. This year there will be a considerable increase in the displays from abroad. Through the agency of the trade fair I think the department is doing useful work in promoting the exchange of goods in a field where effort of that kind is badly needed.
Canadian trade at the present time reveals a number of cross-currents and divergent trends which may well seem confusing. In fact a good many can be traced to the same source- the chronic world shortage of United States dollars. There have been two outstanding considerations in the development of Canadian trade. One is the over-all growth of both exports and imports has increased twofold and threefold in value in the last decade. The other is the increased proportion of our increased trade which we now carry on with the United States. There has been an increase from about fifty per cent in our total world trade in 1939 to 60 per cent of current world trade.
We find that we now have, and I think we can expect to continue to have, a good market for staple products which Canada traditionally
Supply-Trade and Commerce exports, such as wheat, flour, metals, lumber, pulp and paper. These markets seem to be in excellent condition, and we do not expect any particular difficulty with such products. Canadian manufacturers are finding it easier to sell their manufactured goods in the United States than in Europe. I believe that our sales in Europe of manufactured goods depend largely on the amount of effort that is being put behind the selling. During my recent visit to Europe I met vigorous representatives of one of our large farm implement companies in Rome, in Paris, in Belgium and in Holland. As a result of the efforts being put forth by that company its sales in Europe have risen greatly. Because of that kind of selling that company is now the third largest manufacturer of agricultural implements in the world.
Was that from the Canadian plant?

I refer to a Canadian company with foreign subsidiaries, but Canadian exports play a large part in selling on the continent. That company has risen from twelfth place before the war to third place now in the list of farm implement manufacturers in the world.
I am glad to say that in all four capitals I met representatives of the government's own Polymer Corporation. That company is operating at full capacity, and has been since the war, largely as the result of a very active sales program. More than one-third of the rubber produced at that plant is sold in the United Kingdom and in Europe. That, I think, is worth noting at a time when synthetic rubber is being produced greatly in excess of demand and when the price of synthetic rubber is higher than the price of natural rubber. In spite of such handicaps this government-owned corporation is capable of carrying out a selling effort which is disposing of its output, more than one-third of which is going into markets which our manufacturers consider the most difficult in the world.
A pretty good recommendation for public enterprise.

Well, this is different; this is my enterprise. I could give other examples of manufacturers who are selling their products in Europe. They would all be manufacturers who are willing to spend money and effort on selling programs in Europe, and willing to send their top executives there to do the selling rather than third-string sales agents.
Canada must battle for agricultural markets, and in that battle Canada and the United States are handicapped in competing with producers in sterling countries. The dollar

Supply-Trade and Commerce shortage plays its part but there is no indication that the markets are not sufficient to absorb Canadian products as well as those of sterling countries.
What about apples?

That is a bright remark. We are talking billions, and my hon. friends speaks of apples, which incidentally are hardly food. Their main content is water. However, Canadian food products have an excellent position in foreign markets. Our wheat, in particular, is outstanding in quality. It is the preferred wheat in every country in the world. The grades are reliable, the protein content is high, and I have no particular worry about being able to sell Canada's wheat crop.
Our sales are being guided by our Canadian trade commissioner service abroad. We have able men in every country whose duty it is to warn us of market changes and to give us advice on market opportunities. I believe it is remarkable that when one market has been lost through restrictions or for other reasons, these trade commissioners have been able to find outlets for the same products in other markets. The world is wide and we know from experience that the loss of one market does not necessarily mean that no alternate market can be opened up.
One very striking fact is in evidence; the seller's market is over. Today all markets are buyer's markets, and in every market the Canadian exporter meets tough competition. I am glad to say that our price structure in Canada is such that we are well able to meet that competition wherever we encounter it, in the United States or in world markets abroad. It seems to me that a buyer's market is a normal market, and I am not particularly disturbed because of the fact that we are now in a market where the seller really has to work to dispose of his products.
A great deal has been said about Marshall plan dollars. They are not nearly such an important factor in selling today as many would suppose. It is generally considered that to sell in the sterling market, or in any foreign currency markets, there must be Marshall plan dollars. That is not so. The supply of free dollars is increasing all around the world, and each year we are becoming less dependent upon the Marshall plan. Of course that was the purpose of the Marshall plan-to rebuild the economies of the recipient countries so that by the end of 1952 that kind of support would no longer be necessary. A little later I shall say something about the Marshall plan as I saw it in operation at its headquarters in Paris, but I can say that only a very small proportion of our overseas trade

today depends upon Marshall plan dollars, and much of that trade would be carried on if there were no such dollars. It is well to remember that overseas buyers do not purchase Canadian goods just because they love Canada. That may be a factor, but the main reason is that they need the goods. If the goods are needed badly enough, I think there are very few countries that are not able to finance necessary purchases at this time.

It is interesting to note that since the end of the war there has been a total investment in capital equipment-that is in buildings, machinery and production	equipmentamounting to $11,700 million up to the end of 1949. I am afraid I have not that break-down with me today. I have a few notes before me, and I am trying to pick out significant figures as we go along. I will give the hon. member those figures later.
The trend for 1950 is towards a larger proportion in business properties, hospitals and government investment generally. A smaller proportion is going into factories and machinery than was the case in 1949.
One thing that has affected the situation this year, and will continue to do so in 1950, is the drop in agricultural production in 1949. Owing to weather conditions, there was an over-all physical production drop of about ten per cent. The wheat crop was about 26 million bushels less, yet there were 3-4 million acres more in production. Approximately 2-6 million acres had been taken out of other grains, and this, coupled with unfavourable weather conditions, reduced the coarse grain and flaxseed crop by 115 million bushels. The hay crop was about one-quarter less, putting pressure on our dairy producers. This will have its effect on exports in the early part of 1950, because, owing to these short crops, we have not as much to export as we would have had if the crop had been normal.
I should say that our forecasts for 1950 are based on average crops rather than on the subnormal crop that we had last year. If this year's crop is subnormal, the estimates
Supply-Trade and Commerce will be too optimistic; if the crop is above normal, our estimates will be too pessimistic. In referring to agriculture generally, the fivefold increase in farm machinery sales in Canada from $52 million in 1939 to $239 million in 1948 and $255 million in 1949 hardly indicates an agricultural industry that is unduly depressed.
So far as the basic industries of Canada are concerned, the construction industry will have its biggest year in 1950. The newsprint industry is running at capacity for the present, and the indications are that it will do so throughout the year. The pulp market was soft during 1949, but has now strengthened, and Canada's pulp industry is running at full capacity. Indications are that this is likely to continue throughout the year. The lumber industry is in a prosperous condition. To illustrate how conditions change, I may say that last November the lumber industry felt itself to be in a serious condition. I believe that was mentioned in the house. Delegations from both the east and west waited upon the government, pointing out the serious conditions facing that industry. Today, however, the lumber industry is booked to capacity. I am told that industry has sufficient orders to keep it running at capacity for the remainder of the year.
To indicate the position of the west coast lumber industry, tenders were asked by the United Kingdom for 132 million feet of lumber. The west coast mills were unable to quote on the full order, not having unbooked capacity. The United Kingdom fortunately decided to extend the time of delivery and Canadian mills can thus quote on a substantial portion of the order. So far as the east coast is concerned, last autumn we were endeavouring to get the United Kingdom to call for tenders for $2,500,000 worth of eastern lumber from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and eastern Quebec. The call for tenders was delayed, but was finally issued in January and tenders were sent in for about $6 million worth of lumber. Instead of buying the $2,500,000 worth of lumber, the United Kingdom bought the entire $6 million worth. This will keep the eastern lumber industry booked with all it can handle, in addition to supplying the normal United States market and the domestic markets for the remainder of the year.

I found that the countries I visited were becoming less dependent on Marshall aid, and more and more tending in the direction of the return of trade to private enterprise. In Belgium wheat and coarse grains are about the only commodities that are now handled by state agencies. In Italy and France more commodities are being handled by state agencies, but the list of those commodities is being cut down from time to time. There is a return in Europe to private trading, which I think is most favourable to Canadian trade. We in Canada find it easier to do business with private traders, who are concerned only with price and quality, than we do with governments that have other factors in mind.
I found the people in all four countries that I visited were working hard. That was particularly noticeable in driving about the country districts. Every square inch of land was being cultivated. Those who were working the land seemed to be cheerful and happy. Food was plentiful. There were no food restrictions in the countries that I visited. There was plenty of food at reasonable prices. Each of the countries had a population problem. The growth of population has outstripped the productive capacity of the soil. That fact is a worry in all of these countries. Wherever I went I met a discussion of the possibilities of immigration to Canada. We in North America, with plenty of land, are bound to give serious attention to that problem.

I did not visit the United Kingdom. On the day I left Canada an election date was fixed in the United Kingdom. On the day I left Europe the results of the election were known. I thought perhaps the timing was unfavourable for a visit from a Canadian cabinet minister. I had wanted to go to England, but I cancelled that visit.
The threat of communist domination, which was very evident and very serious during my visit in 1947, seems to have been reduced to manageable proportions. There are still large numbers of communists in France and Italy, but they are clearly in the minority. The dividing line has been drawn, and, assuming that the productiveness in those countries can be kept up, provided there is no shortage of food, I think the fear of communist domination in the four countries that I visited was much less than during my visit in 1947. I came back from that earlier visit feeling that there was a possibility that communism would sweep western Europe, as it has swept eastern Europe. I came back this time with a very strong feeling that that would not happen.
I must say that I never had a more enjoyable holiday. My wife and I combined a good rest with most enjoyable contacts with old and new friends in Europe. I hope that I may be privileged to repeat the holiday under similar circumstances before many years go by.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all hon. members have listened for the past hour with intense interest to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Those of us who have spent some years in the house have come to know him as a great optimist. He certainly has been optimistic about Canada's future, at least for the next year. I am quite sure that every hon. member, irrespective of where he sits, hopes that that optimism will be fully realized, and even more.
The minister spoke on the matter of trade and economics and said that they could not very well be separated. I am sure we agree on that point. He spoke on the lack of convertibility of foreign exchange. That is one of the very great problems of this nation today. There is not much argument about that. He dealt at some length with our trade with the United States, and said that it was greater than that of any other two countries in the world. I accept the statement he made. He said that 50 per cent of our exports were to the United States, and 70 per cent of our imports were from that country, and that our adverse trade balance increased from $400 million in 1948 to some $600 million in 1949. He also pointed out that the manufacturers in Canada found it easier to sell in the United States of America than in Europe.

I am sure that most of us are very much concerned about the United States market. The minister also said that there was no trouble in selling Canada's wheat crop. That will also interest very many of us. May I add that the great nation to the south of us produces many of the same types of surpluses that we in Canada do. Especially is that true of agricultural production. Therefore we do have, as the minister said, very many of the same problems, in the matter of looking after foreign markets.
He also said that, as a barometer of agricultural prosperity in this country, farm implement sales had increased fivefold in the past year. They had increased from about $52 million to $230 million. I am sure that anybody who knows our farmers, particularly our western farmers, knows that they are great spenders. If you give them the money they will see that there is prosperity, and money moving in this country. That has been their tradition in Canada up to date.
The minister might have added that the cost of farm implements had increased 12 per cent in Canada during the past year. The estimated requirements of farm implements in Canada in the coming year, which the minister has been so optimistic about, are still over $200 million, and farm implements are still increasing in price. Of the Canadian farm implements 95 per cent are manufactured in eastern Canada. I know we cannot discuss in detail one factor which is going to enter very effectively into the rising cost, namely, freight rates. Increases have taken place in freight rates, and arguments are going on now. That will add considerably to the cost of farm implements. Of the estimated requirements for 1950, 60 per cent of the implements are required in the prairie provinces. Therefore we shall have quite an added cost over last year on these important commodities. That in itself is quite an item.
Our farmers, even sometimes when they have not the wherewithal to purchase these implements, are great buyers. They do try to keep up to date in modern equipment in so far as possible, and they should.
The Canadian people, despite all of this optimism, have a bit of fear about the future. I hope that that fear will not be realized. Some of us have it today. The Canadian people are now realizing that our trade is slipping, to some extent. In 1949 our over-all external trade dropped by about $87 million. In the first two months of this year indications are that our over-all trade was $22 million down, and our trade with the commonwealth $45 million down. I know I cannot discuss this, but measures have been proposed in this house to try to bring about a

trade conference, which I think would be all to the good for our primary products. But the government defeated the proposal.
During the past year we have been very fortunate in that the Marshall aid of the United States-and the minister made some reference to that plan-has helped us. Money was supplied to the extent of several hundred million dollars by the United States, especially in order that Canadian wheat could be supplied to the United Kingdom. Had this all been done otherwise, our trade position with the United Kingdom would have been very different from that set out by the minister.
No.
Wheat could be delivered to them, involving several hundred millions of dollars of Marshall aid money.

Marshall aid money was applied to Canadian wheat; but we would have sold our wheat, whether it had been or not. Marshall aid money for wheat did not help Canada particularly. It did help Great Britain's dollar balance with other countries. The dollar balance with Canada was taken care of in other ways, without Marshall aid.

No, it did not do the
minister's position any harm at all. That plan was made available to Great Britain to take much of our production, and much more wheat than anything else. That is what happened.
Canada is-and we will all agree, including the minister-a great exporting country. Our prosperity certainly depends upon export markets abroad. I pointed out that while we are deeply interested in United States markets, yet the United States and Canada produce many of the same type of surpluses. Therefore we both have to look abroad for trade.

I very much enjoyed listening to the minister this afternoon. He did not seem quite as optimistic as on other occasions in the past. During the first part of his speech in particular, he did give a more balanced picture of many of the factors entering into our export trade. I am glad he had the opportunity of making his trip to Europe; I was happy to hear his report this afternoon, and I am pleased to see him looking so hale and hearty after his journey. I hope Canada's trade in 1950 will be as good as it was in 1949, if not better. I do not want to make any dark predictions as to what will be our trade position. I believe the minister was wise in not attempting to emphasize the disturbing factors too much, because if he had done so he might have caused some panic in this country. At the same time, as far as Canada is concerned, I feel there is a growing pattern of trade that has some dangers in it. We are now, to an ever-increasing extent, tying both our export and import trade to that of the United States; and when we do that, prosperity or otherwise in Canada depends very largely upon conditions prevailing in the United States at any given time. This afternoon the minister stated that early last summer there was a recession in the United States. A recurrence of recession there could have very serious implications as far as Canada is concerned. Many of the things we produce have to compete with commodities produced in the United States; and while I would hope that trade throughout the world will be expanded, I would hope still more that we might see an expansion of trade with Europe, because I believe the policies being followed by many of those governments

would be more likely to bring continuing high levels of trade and prosperity to Canada than we would achieve by tying our trade as we are more and more to that of the United States.
The minister went on to state that he expected exports to the United Kingdom from Canada this year to be down. He also said that the shortage of dollars is causing many European countries to adopt restrictive trade practices. He further stated that perhaps Canada would be able to come through the present period of readjustment with only a few scars. I believe that statement is correct. I only hope that the sections of Canada that get the scars will not be those sections that have always gotten the scars in the past, when any readjustment was taking place. I refer in particular to the industry of agriculture. While our export trade with Europe may be good on balance, nevertheless certain sections of agriculture have suffered and are suffering because of a falling off in the European market. The other evening the Minister of Finance stated, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said today, that while our markets in Europe for grain have continued at a high level, there has been a drop in the markets for animal products, timber and certain other commodities.
In the world as we have it today I do not believe we should have to worry about agricultural surpluses. I noticed what the minister said in reference to European countries whose populations were increasing, and his statement that they would have a continuing and growing problem of feeding those populations. Then he went on to say that this presented an immigration problem to Canada. I agree with that statement; and I believe that a country as wealthy as Canada should accept its responsibilities in the world. But I do not believe that immigration to Canada by people from European countries is necessarily the whole or the main solution. When we have certain agricultural surpluses in Canada, and when the United States has huge agricultural surpluses, those surpluses should be made available to the European countries. That would remove some of the pressure against European food resources.
The minister quoted figures to show that Canada's trade position with the United Kingdom over the whole of 1949 was better to the extent of an increase of $20 million in exports. He also made note of the fact that Canadian exports to European countries declined by about $90 million. I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce took a more realistic attitude this afternoon than that taken by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech
Supply-Trade and Commerce last fall. In referring to devaluation during that speech the Minister of Finance said at page 974 of Hansard of October 20, 1949:
It was agreed that the solution must be sought primarily in a rapid and substantial increase in dollar earnings through an expansion of trade.
The simple facts presented by the minister this afternoon show that, in the last few months since devaluation, there has been no increase in Canadian dollars earned by European countries. As a matter of fact, if I may quote what I said in the budget debate last fall, I feel I came a lot closer than the Minister of Finance to hitting the mark. My remarks are found on page 1335 of Hansard of November 1, 1949:
I contend that devaluation, instead of bringing about an expansion of trade, will in fact bring about a contraction in trade. A 30 per cent devaluation of the pound sterling in relation to United States dollars means an increased price of 44 per cent to the British consumer of goods bought in the United States. That is certainly going to mean a substantial reduction of British purchases of United States goods. The same thing will be true to a slightly lesser extent in British purchases of Canadian goods.
Then with respect to the British attempt to increase exports to this continent. Great Britain following devaluation can reduce by 30 per cent the price of her exports to the United States. But should Great Britain, for example, reduce the export price of British automobiles to the United States by 30 per cent, then she must increase the quantity exported to the United States by 43 per cent in order to obtain the same number of dollars that she has been receiving before devaluation. It is certainly doubtful to what extent Great Britain can increase her earnings of United States and Canadian dollars by reduction of price, since following reduction in price she must increase the quantity sold to earn even the same number of dollars as she earned heretofore.
Rather, I believe the chief result of devaluation will be a further loss of the British market.
In the budget address the other night, the Minister of Finance told us that in the last four months there had been a decline in our exports to the United Kingdom by an amount of $20 million, and our imports from the United Kingdom were down by $3 million. Our overseas exports as a whole, however, were down by more than $100 million in the first four months; and our overseas imports by $92 million. In my opinion devaluation, instead of bringing about a better balance of trade, made it worse and has substantially reduced our exports to European markets. It has not increased the amount of dollars earned by European countries. I trust the government will take all necessary steps to increase our imports from European countries. I hope our exports to the United Kingdom will not fall during the coming year, as was forecast by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Our exports to the United Kingdom and other European countries should be maintained, and if we want them maintained

Supply-Trade and Commerce then we need to increase our purchases of British goods. I hope the government will place greater emphasis on increasing our imports of British goods, rather than allowing the adjustment to come about through a reduction of our exports.
This afternoon the minister said there would be a battle for agricultural markets in the future. I believe that statement is correct. Our farmers are willing to help in that battle for the British market and other European markets. Our farmers purchased $255 million worth of farm machinery this past year, and they would be most willing to buy increased quantities of British machinery if by so doing they were guaranteed a market in Britain for bacon, eggs, cheese and other agricultural commodities. While the government has so far turned its back on the idea of a bilateral trade agreement, nevertheless I feel that such a trade agreement, by means of which farm machinery could be exchanged for farm products at present in surplus, would receive the wholehearted support of organized agriculture.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that the Marshall plan was not as large an* item now in support of trade as it was in the past, but I suggest that the importance of Marshall plan aid should not be minimized. It could be important in getting a market for Canadian agricultural products, but if used the wrong way it could be a factor in taking from us the markets that we now have. It has been suggested by the foreign affairs committee of the United States house of representatives that of the $2,750 million to be voted this year for Marshall aid, $1 billion should be earmarked for the purchase of United States agricultural surpluses. If such a move were made, then Marshall plan dollars would make our market problem much greater than it is today. In order to try to insulate us from this sort of policy that might arise from time to time, and over which we have no control, I feel that the government, through an export-import board, should be increasing its role in international trade. Then, if the United States decided to do something like that, we would have a much safer hold on our markets than we have at present.
I noticed the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the prospects for marketing wheat and other grains in Europe were good for this year. I hope he is right. I should like to quote to him, however, the first paragraph of the Canadian wheat board report for the year ending July 31, 1949. It says: Increased production of wheat in Europe, ample wheat supplies available in exporting countries, the intensity of United States competition, the imme-
diate effects of United States aid to various countries in western Europe and increasing difficulties in financing international trade, were important factors in the 1948-49 wheat position.
Along with that, I should like to point out to the minister that today the United States has a surplus of more than 475 million bushels of wheat. Then, I might ask him why the Minister of Agriculture suggested that western farmers reduce their wheat acreage by 3 million acres, if the markets for wheat and other grains are available, while the markets for secondary agricultural products are falling? Either the advice of the Minister of Agriculture was not sound or else the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce today, that our wheat market is assured, does not jibe with the actual prospects. I do not think there can be a reconciliation between the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture that wheat acreage should be reduced and the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that wheat and grain markets are secure.
We in this group supported the British wheat agreement. We also supported the international wheat agreement and we trust that it will work throughout the whole period which is for the next three years. We know that under the British wheat agreement we obtained a large share of the British market. But when we did that, we sacrificed some of the markets we had once had in countries on the European continent. For example, France in 1936 imported from Canada
6,250,000	bushels of wheat and last year did not import any Canadian wheat. Belgium, in 1936, imported 16 million bushels of wheat from Canada and last year imported just over 5 million bushels. Denmark, in 1936, imported from Canada almost 5 million bushels of wheat and last year imported only 4,567 bushels from Canada. The Netherlands, in 1936, imported over 7 million bushels from Canada and last year imported less than half a million bushels. We are going to have to maintain a market in Britain for the present quantity of wheat that is going to Britain, namely, 140 million bushels a year; or, if we are relegated in the British market to our 1930 position, then it is imperative that action be taken towards securing for Canada a better position in the European markets. The fact is that today Canada is supplying little of the wheat going to those traditional markets.
When I began my remarks I said that I hoped the Minister of Trade and Commerce would say that oats, barley and wheat at least, and preferably all grains, would be handled solely by the wheat board. As I have said before, the wheat pool organizations and the farm organizations in western Canada are not satisfied with the government's oats and barley

policy in its entirety. They are glad that the wheat board accepts delivery of all oats and barley produced in western Canada but, as was shown by the Saskatchewan wheat pool in convention last fall, they are opposed to the speculative market being continued in the disposition of oats and barley.
I noticed that the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day, in announcing that there would be no wheat board payment this year-that is, before the end of the wheat pool period-said that one of the contributing factors was the stand taken by the opposition.
I believe that is dodging the real reason why a payment is not being made. In my opinion, the real reason why a payment is not being made is that the wheat board has not large sums of money on hand with which to make a payment. A further factor is that farmers object strenuously to the wheat board's going to the banks and paying on money borrowed from the banks an interest rate five times as high as the rate earned by the wheat board on money it invests in Dominion of Canada treasury bills.
What I objected to in a previous speech was the fact that, before the 1948 wheat payment was made, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that "the payment is being made out of money now available in the wheat board fund." The Minister of Agriculture went further and said that the farmers would not want the government to borrow money in order to make a payment over and above the 20 cents a bushel. Then, during the same debate, the Minister of Agriculture made the statement that 20 cents a bushel would be provided for a further year.
I should like to quote what the Minister of Agriculture said, as reported at page 1720 of Hansard of February 27, 1948:
Under the plan of five-year payments that was brought into effect in 1945 the farmer knows that if there is drought he will have more money coming to him at an increase of twenty cents in each year, no matter when that drought comes.
I say that was a clear indication by the Minister of Agriculture that there would be a further large payment made this year and this spring. There has been no worse crop failure situation in western Canada for a long time than that which prevailed during last fall. The farmers need an additional payment now much more than they needed it at certain times in the past. I might say that I have had a great deal of correspondence from farmers as to the wheat payment, or the fact that there will be no wheat payment, and the method by which the government went about making that payment. In that respect I should like to quote a letter I received from Mr. Ed.
31, 1950
Supply-Trade and Commerce McBride, secretary of the wheat pool committee at Viceroy, Saskatchewan. In writing to me he said:
The farmers at Viceroy are very much disturbed by the rumours from Ottawa regarding our final payment from the wheat board.
When the 20-cent a bushel payment was made a year ago, we didn't hear anything of a bank loan being made to help make it. In fact, we were told there was still a large surplus left after the payment was made.
During last summer and fall different experts estimated the probable amount of the final wheat board payment to farmers at from 17J cents to as high as 26 cents a bushel. Now they are saying we will only get a few cents a bushel.
I believe the government should be strongly criticized for having raided the wheat board fund in order to make a 20-cent additional payment just before an election, without telling the farmers that by doing so the wheat board would have to go substantially into debt. I would ask the minister, as I have already done, to continue the wheat price at not less than $1.75 per bushel and to increase* barley prices to $1.20 per bushel and oats to 90 cents per bushel. I trust that the minister's optimistic forecasts will be proven right. I hope we may obtain markets during the coming year at least as great as those we obtained during the past year; but I hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government will adopt policies to increase our imports from European countries and that any adjustment that is finally necessary in our trading pattern will be brought about in such a way as not to bring scars to the agricultural industry.

I do not think that during this session this house has heard a more important announcement than that made today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. After all, the whole prosperity of this country depends on whether or not our trade will be preserved during the months and years that lie ahead. The striking thing is that, while the minister spoke on so important a subject, few, if any, of his colleagues in the cabinet found it of sufficient importance to be in the house. I was particularly surprised at the fact, for which no doubt there is a very good reason, that the Minister of Agriculture was not present on this occasion, particularly when the discussion that will take place will necessarily be concerned to a considerable extent with the marketing of agricultural products. Wheat and its marketing are of very great importance not only to the farmers of western Canada but also to our economy as a whole.
First, I want to refer to a matter about which I asked some questions this afternoon. The hon. member for Assiniboia mentioned
1442	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce the situation in the prairie provinces. According to a report of the Department of Agriculture the drought situation in 1949 was the most serious in a period of eleven years of western Canada's history. If there is one thing more than another that has been emphasized by the western farmer in recent months it has been the need of having an interim payment made of the moneys in the hands of the wheat pool operated by the wheat board of this country.
It has been alleged that some members of the opposition criticized the payment last spring of 20 cents a bushel. I heard no such criticism from the official opposition, but the fact is that the payment was timed to be made in advance of the election. When it was made was there no suggestion that the money was being dispersed in a considerable measure from moneys borrowed by the wheat board?
. When the Minister of Agriculture spoke in Moose Jaw in April, 1949, he advised the farmers that there was an additional amount to their credit of from 12 cents to 15 cents a bushel at that time. That statement could scarcely have been correct, for now we find that in order to make the payment the wheat board had to borrow moneys and did not have to the credit of the farmer at that time 33 cents to 35 cents, or even 20 cents, the amount advanced.
Is there not a difference between cash in the till and the actual credit position of the pool?
The statement-
There is the working capital item. The wheat board has to borrow its working capital.
That is not the position. It was said that the money was available in the pool, and not that the pool had the credit and would be able to secure that much money.
Not the cash.

At that time the minister said that the wheat board had on hand in addition to the 20-cent advance from 12 cents to 15 cents a bushel to the credit of the farmer, which is a long way from saying that it would have to borrow in order to meet the situation.
He did not say that we had it in cash.

No, he did not say, "we have it in cash". He said, "we have it available". Certainly when it is in credit it is not available, according to the interpretation placed on those words by the farmers in western Canada.
If the pool had stopped doing business that day it would have been available.
Mr. Chairman, the farmer was told it was there. The farmer was not told that the 20 cents was borrowed, or any part of it, in order to make the payment in advance of an election.
It was not.
It was borrowed-
The consolidated revenue fund is available at that rate.

What the farmers cannot understand is why that money had to be borrowed to make the payment for the amount the farmer will ultimately secure will be reduced by the very large amount paid out in interest.
To help in the election.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the fact that it was paid out just in advance of the election was, as you and I know, merely coincidental.	[DOT]

I am making another appeal to the minister in connection with an interim payment. I know he has made a decision on the matter and the wheat board have; but if he could see the letters hon. members from western Canada receive regarding this matter he would reconsider it in respect of the areas that were stricken with drought last year. The areas are readily identifiable. If payment could be made in those areas in advance of seeding operations it would indeed be appreciated by tens of thousands of farmers who find themselves in a position where they are unable to get credit. I again make that appeal, as I have over the past several weeks, that the minister reconsider it. I could give the minister, if he would care to read them, at least a hundred letters which have come in within the last week from farmers, particularly of central and southern Saskatchewan, who because of drought conditions last year doubt their ability to purchase their requirements and seed their land again in the next three or four weeks in the hope and expectation of a crop. I do not make this request as a general appeal for all of the western provinces, but for those areas where there was an almost complete failure in 1949.
There is one other matter that I should like to bring to the minister's attention. I asked a question today in connection with feed oats. After I had asked the question I received a letter from a dairy farmer who

points out that on March 27 he endeavoured to buy No. 1 feed oats, and he had to pay 93 cents a bushel for them.
From what point was this?

At Qu'Appelle, near
Regina. He said, "the price has been fixed by the wheat board." He points out that the farmer received 50 cents a bushel, and that there is a further 10 cents a bushel coming from the wheat board, according to the figures given to the house some weeks ago by the minister. What the farmers out there want to know is this. What about that extra amount of 33 cents a bushel? Who receives that? They also ask the federal government to protect them against having to pay a price per bushel 33 cents more than the farmer will receive from the wheat board for No. 1 feed oats that he has sold to them.

Perhaps my hon. friend would not mind my clearing up that point. It is quite legal for a farmer at Qu'Appelle to buy from any other farmer at Qu'Appelle. The price of oats at Qu'Appelle is the Fort William price less freight, and the Fort William price is-
Ninety cents.
Not for oats; it is 61J cents.
That is right.

It is 61 \ cents, less freight, which will bring it to about 50 cents at Qu'Appelle. Unless he had the oats railed back from Fort William I cannot imagine how he got the price up to 90 cents. It does not make sense.

That is exactly it. I cannot understand it, and neither can the minister. After I asked the question before the orders of the day this afternoon I received a letter from another farmer pointing out the unfairness to the dairy farmers in Saskatchewan in having to pay a price of 93 cents for No. 1 feed oats.
Perhaps my hon. friend can clear it up by writing back and asking who the vendor was.
I can give the name of the vendor, but I shall not do so in the committee. It is one of the elevator companies.
I cannot believe an elevator company at that point-

It is a matter which the minister should look into. I have given the facts, and I can give him the letter. I say it is unjust that a price such as that should be charged for feed oats to western farmers.

The western farmer is charged the Winnipeg price-not the floor price of the
Supply-Trade and Commerce wheat board. He is charged the Winnipeg price plus whatever handling charges there are. Oats are selling away over the floor. The Winnipeg price today is about 90 cents, and the farmer has to pay 90 cents plus elevator charges.
And that seems most unfair.
He could buy from any other farmer. The farmer in that area would sell to the elevator company or to the dairy at the same price.

If we are going to encourage trade between Great Britain and Canada, if Canada is to be assured agricultural markets in the United Kingdom, we should do everything we can to encourage purchases of heavy machinery and the like in Great Britain. It is not a simple problem, and the minister, with all his experience, will certainly be the first to agree. I do feel that if the demoralizing influence of bilateral trade is continued and we build up in this world three blocs and two ideologies, the hope of peace dreamed of in San Francisco in 1945 will indeed evaporate.
I repeat there should be more co-operation between the minister's department and the Department of National Revenue to encourage the purchase of British goods in Canada. A few months ago our Canadian National Railways were unable to operate because of a shortage of coal. I am not saying that British coal could be used for the operation of our locomotives, but it could have taken the place of coal that was used for that purpose.
We buy every pound of coal that we can get in England.
That is not what was said by a British member recently who stated that there was no reason why Great Britain could not supply us with a million tons a year.
For three years we have been begging for coal from Britain.
I am just quoting what a Labour member said in the British House of Commons when dealing with this question.
Perhaps he is as careless with his facts as our Labour members.

That is a private feud and I am not going to get into it. As one who is looking at this problem in the general way that a person of my training would, I would ask the minister what has been done about canvassing the manufacturers in Canada in order to find out what they can buy in Great Britain.
We have been over it with a fine-tooth comb.

We have not been told about it then. I should like the minister to tell the house and the country whether our import defence requirements are being purchased in the United Kingdom to the greatest extent possible. I have read a number of articles published in the United States, one recently in an outstanding journal, to the effect that Canada is not purchasing her defence requirements in the United Kingdom to the extent she should.
