AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. May-bank for the second reading of Bill No. 7, respecting Alberta Natural Gas Company, and the motion of Mr. MacDougall: "That this question be now put."

Mr. Speaker, in concluding my remarks on this bill tonight I should like to re-emphasize that there has been on my part-and having followed this debate closely I think I can say with accuracy that there has been on the part of others who have spoken in opposition to this and the other bill-no suggestion that we are opposed to the eventual export of gas and oil to the United States. All we have asked for, and what we are still asking for, is that before our gas and oil goes to the United States market the line transporting it should pass through Canadian territory and serve Canadian industries and cities along its maximum length before crossing the border into the United States. Indeed, we have been careful to make it clear that there is no suggestion that we should attempt to curtail the export of these resources to the United States after Canadian needs have been met.
I refer to this because I noticed a report in the Vancouver Daily Province of Saturday, March 25, appearing at page 3, commenting on some remarks made by myself and other hon. members during this debate. That report contains this passage:
Mr. Fulton said he would not oppose the bills if the government saw fit to amend the original Pipe
1446	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Alberta Natural Gas Company Lines Act in such a way that Canadian oil could not be exported into the U.S.
He had received representations from various segments of industry in his constituency, including chambers of commerce, appealing to him to see that the oil and gas did not leave this country.
I said no such thing on the occasion referred to. I made no suggestion that the main act should be amended in the way suggested in the newspaper report. What I said, and what I repeat, was that as far as I was concerned if the government would see fit to amend the main pipe-line act so that any company seeking incorporation to build an oil or gas pipe line must build it for its maximum length through Canada first, before it crossed the border, I would not oppose the incorporation of any company that wished to obtain a charter to build a line under those terms. The position has been made so clear by those of us who have spoken in opposition to these two bills-that what we are seeking to do is serve Canada first but not serve Canada only, and not deny the export of gas to the United States-that I cannot understand how any report in the press could become so confused. As a matter of fact what I said on the occasion referred to was that if the government would amend the original act in the way I suggested, quoting Hansard at page 1109:
-we would be content to grant incorporation to as many companies as wish to build the line through Canada first.
That cannot be taken in any way as a suggestion that we should deny the ultimate export of these resources to the United States, after our own needs have been met.
In conclusion I want to refer to a little history which I think will be of interest to the house, and which I know will be of interest to my colleagues from British Columbia, though in this case they may not agree with the opinions expressed. In the course of my reading during this debate I went back to the debates at the time of the incorporation and construction of the Canadian Pacific railway, in order to see what was said then as to the need for building this great line through Canada to serve Canada first and build up a nation north of the 49th parallel. I found this very interesting remark in a speech delivered by Sir Charles Tupper in 1882. I am going to read it so that hon. members may see why I feel it to be so important that this pipe line go through our own territory. As I say, other hon. members may not altogether agree with the sentiments expressed; in fact I think Sir Charles was a little off in some of his geography, though not in his sentiments. He was off in his geography, of course, because he did not have the advantage which is available now to all horn 
members of visiting our province and, in particular, my district. Referring to the proposal that the Canadian Pacific railway should go through the Kicking Horse pass and down through what we call the interior of British Columbia, he said:
This is a matter which would be of great importance not only to the line but to the country, because it would penetrate the best district in British Columbia, that is the Kamloops district-
There is an unsolicited testimonial that was delivered in 1882. With the support of so great an authority as Sir Charles Tupper, one of the founders of confederation, I think hon. members will see why I am so anxious, together with all my colleagues from British Columbia on this side of the house and one on the other side, that this line should be built through British Columbia, through Canada first.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not delay lion, members long, but I have something to say that has not been said as yet. The other day I heard the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) made a good speech; that is, it was good for the opposition. He was trying to convince the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) that it would be a good thing for the country if he were to appoint a committee of this house. Well, Mr. Speaker, if it is a good thing for the national defence of this country to have a committee, it is a good thing for the development of our natural resources to have a committee. We have a committee and, Mr. Speaker, I think it is an intelligent committee, worthy of being trusted. Any man who stands up in this house and says that we should not trust that committee is asking us not to trust him. Some of these men who do not want the resources of Alberta to be developed are saying, "Do not trust me because I shall sell you down the river."
When I look over this committee, I find the name of the member for Yancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I think he is worthy of being trusted. I trust him with the development of the natural resources of this country. Then, there is the member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy); a high-school teacher, and an intelligent man. Yet he is asking this house not to trust the committee of which he is a member. The member for Queens (Mr. McLure) is another member of the committee.
I think he is an intelligent man, and worthy of being trusted; a good committee man. I believe we can trust this committee to do this work. If there was ever a time in the history of this house when I believe the government would be justified in forcing closure, it is now.
The people in the country are asking this question. They are asking what is behind

this opposition to the pipe line. I know there is gas behind it, and there is oil; and so far as I can see the gas will not be sold without the oil, because the province of Alberta is wise enough, according to the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), not to remove the pressure of the gas and thus lose the oil. As I have said, this committee should be trusted, but I expect that even after I have spoken there will be a lot of people who will say we should develop the natural resources of this country for Canada; we should save them for future generations. To them I would say, why ship wheat to England? Why not turn the wheat into flour in Canada, and ship the flour?
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the best thing to do is to develop the natural resources of our country. We should have the gas and oil from our country meet the gas and oil from the south, so that the people who are asking for this gas and oil can have it. I say, send this bill along; develop the natural resources of our country, and cure any unemployment we have.
Hon. W. Earl Rowe (Dufferin-Simcoeb Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). At times I feel he is almost my representative, because I am responsible for a large industry in his riding. I have been surprised that he has not been struggling to give us Alberta oil in place of United States coal to help support that industry. That is a matter of his judgment, however, or lack of judgment; I know he is sincere in his conviction, so I do not want to be too critical of him.
While I represent a district somewhat removed from the particular district in which the most direct benefits will accrue from the utilization of that great resource in Alberta, I feel that it is rather encouraging to find so many people in this house interested in this oil in Alberta. No similar number of people in the world enjoy the bountiful resources that we do in Canada. I do feel that there is probably only one real issue at stake. I have listened to those who are familiar with the problem this issue presents, and I find there is only one real contention. It seems to be whether this pipe line is going to be built through Canada first, or is going through the United States first. There is no use in talking about technicalities, or this commission or that commission, or what the provinces have to do. This line can be built through Canada first if this house so wishes.
This is a private bill, but it is rather interesting to note the keen concern and support the government has given it. I know there are members of the government, who are absent tonight, who have not been very active
31, 1950	1447
Alberta Natural Gas Company in the debate. I know there is one hon. member from British Columbia who has taken an active part in the debate. I feel that the members from the other provinces are here to form a national representation. After all, this is the forum that represents this great nation. I feel rather keenly that we are dealing with an issue that can mean a great deal in the years that lie ahead. The trend of our development in this country, Mr. Speaker, is interlocked with the great possibilities that surround this issue. While I am still not perhaps as old as the oldest member in the house, in the last quarter century I have seen great changes in the trend of the development of this young nation. I can recall when any man aspiring to parliament would speak of agriculture as the basic industry of Canada; the backbone of the country.
I well recall saying, on one occasion back in 1927, that at some time we might find it difficult to sell our wheat. Some of the members from western Canada laughed at me and said, "You do not know much about western Canada's ability to produce; you will never see wheat below a dollar a bushel. We will always be an agricultural country. We control the bread basket of the world." Since that time, Mr. Speaker, as you have observed, that trend has changed far more rapidly than our fathers ever dreamed it would change. Today we have a country, perhaps showing the effects of two great wars, that has been industrialized until now rural activities make up only about 30 per cent of our national enterprise. Canada has rapidly become an industrial country. Canada is a cold country, Mr. Speaker. Its climate is different from that of the southern states, and many other places. More than anything else, Canada needs food and clothing. If this country is to have a well-rounded economy, it must encourage the production of those things essential to a high standard of living. As every hon. member knows, there is nothing much more important to the women and children of poor families across this dominion than warm clothing and a warm house. Fuel, in other words, is a problem in many districts. We in this country have for years depended on many million dollars' worth of United States coal. We have been importing large amounts of it. We know that today there is no fuel on the North American continent that can compete with natural gas. That fact has been proven across the line. We know that with high wages, with coal being shipped for long distances, and with freight rates increasing, the price of coal is ever on the advance.
We know that if we are going to develop this country in competition with that great republic to the south of us, we must do as it has done. While we will listen to the Minister

Alberta Natural Gas Company of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and other people make statements about the great development or the great markets we have in the United States, with which we all agree, nevertheless, we are similar to the United States in many respects. We produce similar agricultural products and similar industrial products and we are more or less in competition with them.
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Ontario where we have had the greatest industrial development has been where we have had the power, where we have had hydroelectric developments and where we have had coal, just as old England and other countries overseas in the last century developed great industrial progress and led the world in industry because they had the horsepower and the fuel. They had the steam-generating plants and what drove them and made the country great. Therefore not only is this great potential resource important but it is vital to this young dominion for household needs, for providing the horsepower requirements of the industrial plants, and for commerce in general. Remember, Mr. Speaker, that coal to heat a house costs twice as much money as natural gas. We might look across the border to the south of us and take a lesson from there, because no matter how much experience you may have had or how you have watched this country grow, if you want to foresee the future of Canada you can see it better in the light of what has developed just across the border.
It is said that the nineteenth century belonged to the United States. That great leader of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier-I think he was the greatest they have ever had; I have not seen any since that ever came up to him-said that the nineteenth century was the United States' but the twentieth century would be Canada's. There is no one worthy of being in this house who cannot visualize that greatness in the future and who cannot realize what is happening.
I can well remember that, when I first entered the House of Commons, our annual budgets were under $400 million. Now they ire $2,400 million. Our national income now is $16 billion; the difference is greater perhaps in high inflationary dollars than in physical volume, but nevertheless it shows the trend of the times.
We have a small population but, in fairness, it must be admitted that we are making great progress with that small population. While the United States of America has since before the war had an increase in population which is more than our total population, nevertheless, percentagewise, we are keeping reasonable pace with them. Because of our

great resources, the power and the potential reserves such as Alberta gas and oil, even the weaknesses of the present government cannot deter great progress in this country. We have a great country, and a virile and hardy people; and I am satisfied that this country will grow, as has the United States of America, even though parts of it are a little bit colder than parts of the United States.
The United States' experience has shown that the most rapid-growing and spectacular industry on the North American continent at the present time, is the gas and oil industry. We have other great industries but the one that has been most dramatic, the most rapid in development, and the one that is now most spectacular in its relationship to our North American economy is the gas and oil industry. I cite here North American development because, after all, we are very similar. We are closely allied in relationship to the United States of America. We live beside the United States. Although there is that invisible line that separates us, we are tied together in customs, in trade and in national defence; we are tide together in outlook and in aspirations. I can see that, in the future, that close relationship with that great republic and with the British commonwealth of nations offers the greatest hope for security and peace. By the very fact that the people in the United States are annually investing about $1 billion in their gas and oil development they have shown that they realize what it means. The volume of gas and oil transported by the United States pipe lines from the far south into the more thickly populated areas has increased; from 1940 to 1948 it doubled. There is a $3 billion plan now under way in the next five years, and it is estimated that in the next three years it will be double that. There is a country that has great experience in development; it is the greatest industrial country in the world; and it developed with resources and people similar to those we have in this country.
Gas and oil.

Gas and oil. At the present time a 2,000-mile gas line is being built from Texas into the New York section. The domestic sales of gas to householders in the United States now amount to a billion dollars a year. Householders to the number of 15 million are served by gas. Gas is being used even in those areas close beside great potential deposits of coal that we are importing here into Canada. Much of what is involved in this issue is national energy and power; it is not only a question of fuel but of power for industry. Today the United States of

America, with its gas lines, provides to householders as well as to industry, through gas pipe lines, almost three times as much power as it does through all its vast water powers. Realizing what our great hydro developments have meant to the old province of Ontario,
I can visualize in years to come what the gas pipe lines and the oil development of the western provinces of Canada may mean to them in the next twenty-five years.
We are challenged here, Mi. Speaker, as representatives of this dominion, to pause and realize whether we should divert these lines and send this great potential natural power over to the United States before it serves our Canadian people. I know that someone may say that is not exactly the issue, that they can build the line wherever they like, and that all we need to settle this whole argument is for those of the government who seem to be so interested in this private bill to tell us that this line is going to be built in Canada first, to serve Canadians first and then serve the people of the United States later, just as the United States would do if the positions were reversed. Forty-nine per cent or almost half of all the national energy and power for the industries of that vast country to the south of us is obtained from oil and gas and only four per cent is hydroelectric power or water power.
The question therefore has been considered to be an issue in that country. The fact that in the last twelve years twelve times as much money has been spent in the development of these transcontinental gas lines in the United States is indicative of the possibilities for the future. There are the United States Pipe Lines, Panhandle Eastern Pipe Lines, New York and Richmond Pipe Lines, Transcontinental Gas Transmission Pipe Lines Incorporated, Texas Eastern Pipe Lines and Tennessee Pipe Lines and many others. For instance, the Transcontinental lines alone in the United States spent $191 million before they had a dollar of revenue. The soundest investment houses in the United States, the Boston Mutual, the Metropolitan Life and the leading financiers of the United States, grabbed these securities and gave them bonds at good rates because they saw the possibilities of cheaper heat and power. Surely we in Canada, Mr. Speaker, should realize what it could mean to this country when the great republic to the south of us is piping gas almost two thousand miles; and they are ready to back that investment privately and otherwise. I ask, Mr. Speaker, should we not pause? I ask the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), does he criticize us now for pausing to discuss whether we are going to send Alberta oil over to the United States first? Are we going to let Alberta oil

Personally I am glad to see that there are several companies ready to build pipe lines. We shall have no trouble getting the gas transported. There will be no trouble to get these lines built.
As the hon. member has just said, it does not matter how many lines you may approve. We are not opposing the building of a pipe line. I have no axe to grind, Mr. Speaker. I do not know the personalities in either case, but I feel that I would be derelict in my responsibilities as a member of this house if I did not do everything in my power to see that these lines were developed east and west rather than north and south to start with. I am satisfied that there are greater possibilities in western Canada than many people have yet dreamed of.
In many parts of the United States the domestic requirements are now beyond the supply. Utility companies are asking the governing bodies to restrict the use of gas for domestic purposes, because they cannot build the pipe lines as rapidly as needed to serve the people who want the gas from down in the far south. Gas is an exhausting resource. I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that the future population of this country is not 15 million but 50 million. I have every confidence that in another 25 years, with the progress that you have observed in the last quarter of a century, you will see in Canada the greatest development going on in any place in the world. I am sure that western Canada will be a great industrial centre. It is bound to be. That development will not come by chance. That development will not come by saying that all is well. That development will not come by saying that, if the opposition will keep quiet and not face the dangers of the future, all will be well and we shall be prosperous. You know, Mr. Speaker, that development will come where there are great resources. People live where they can sustain a high standard of living. People seek employment where there are great resources and possibilities. History has shown that there is no greater factor in the development of any country than the possibilities of power. In the old days it was coal; then it was hydroelectric power; and now we are in the oil and gas age. The fact is that the United States of America is now leaning more towards that, and it shows the possibilities that we have in the years that lie ahead.
Natural gas costs little more than one-half manufactured gas. As I have said, the recent development of Alberta gas and oil is, to my mind, the most spectacular single feature of hope in our rapidly changing Canadian

Alberta Natural Gas Company economy. I do believe that there is a tendency to feel more or less inferior to the United States of America. I take second place to no one in this house in my admiration for the great advancement of the republic to the south of us, the great market for many of our products. When the United States is prosperous, as it is at the present time, Canada, with about only one-tenth of the population, with similar customs, is bound to be prosperous.
I do feel-and I believe it has been the policy of the party to which I belong-that Canadian resources should be developed first for the benefit of Canadian people. I know that some of my hon. friends across the way used to be free traders. Now they are not just sure what they are. I know there are those on the front benches across the way who will say we must look north and south. One extreme is perhaps as bad as the other. But I am satisfied now that even those who believed in free trade a few years ago, and believed in building north and south and in supporting the United States and keeping us, as has so often been said, hewers of wood and drawers of water, in this advanced age do not want to ibe diggers of gas and oil for the benefit of developing the great western state of Washington ahead of British Columbia or Alberta. Not long ago I noticed a United States writer said that that would be the next state developed in the United States. Since we have found a great bonanza of gas and oil in the province of Alberta, if they can get the pipe line down through the United States they will develop Washington as they have indicated.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
That a select committee be appointed on radio broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies and aims of the corporation and its regulations, revenues, expenditures and development, with power to examine and inquire into the matters and things herein referred to and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and to send for persons, papers and records:
That the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable or necessary;
That the committee have power to meet while the house is sitting;
That the committee shall consist of the following members: Messrs, Baker, Boisvert, Cote (St. Johns-Iberville-Napierville), Decore, Diefenbaker, Fleming, Fulton, Gauthier (Portneuf), Gauthier (Sudbury), Hansell, Henry, Isnor, Kent, Knight, Langlois (Gaspe), Maybank, McCann, Murray (Cariboo), Richard (Ottawa East), Robinson, Riley, Smith (Moose Mountain), Smith (Calgary West), Stewart (Winnipeg North), and Whitman;
That the presence of at least nine members shall be a quorum of the said committee; and
That standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some brief remarks on this resolution to set up a select committee on radio broadcasting. Since the national radio system was started in 1932 different governments have thought it appropriate that committees of the house: should be appointed from time to time to study the activities of the system and to. consider general broadcasting questions. Through the years different committees have formulated principles upon which broadcasting in Canada is based. They have also made a number of important recommendations which have been carried out following their reports.	.
We believe it is a good thing to have committees on broadcasting such as that proposed in this resolution. Broadcasting is different from most other public activities. Parliament long ago decided that broadcasting should be entrusted to a public corporation having a wide degree of independence of the executive government. There were two important reasons for this: first, that broadcasting,
1454

Radio Broadcasting
which is quite different from ordinary government administration, should be carried on by a corporation able to follow many of the methods of private enterprise in its work and having the necessary flexibility in its operations; second, that broadcasting, carrying as it does much information and opinion, should be run by an independent and impartial body which would be free from any question of partisan influence.
Under the Canadian Broadcasting Act the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not answerable to me or the government for its actions in carrying on its broadcasting operations, and the government is not responsible for the actions of the corporation in carrying on its broadcasting under the act. The corporation is of course responsible to the overall jurisdiction of parliament. In effect it reports directly to parliament as a whole. That is why it is particularly appropriate that a committee of this house composed of members of all parties should examine the activities of the corporation.
The government does support the principle of a strong, national, publicly-owned broadcasting system independent of any possible partisan influence, flexible in its structure and in its methods. This is a principle agreed upon by all major political parties in the past, and we believe approved by the vast majority of Canadian citizens. The corporation itself is independently responsible for its daily actions in carrying out its trust. It seems fitting, therefore, that a committee of parliament should examine the reports of the activities and plans of the corporation, and get information and explanations which it wishes directly from its officers.
Under the broadcasting act the government has a responsibility for approving large capital commitments by the corporation. Since the war we have approved the establishment of facilities to extend or improve the services to the people of Canada in different areas. We have also provided loans for other purposes. These developments have been all moves toward the kind of national coverage which was always envisaged for this particular system. New transmitters in Alberta, Manitoba, southern Ontario and the Saguenay district went into operation in 1948. Last year a new medium power station was added on Cape Breton island, which it is hoped to improve in the future. This year a new 10 kilowatt station will go into operation near Windsor to bring national service for the first time to the people of southwestern Ontario. The power of station CBM, serving English-language listeners in the province of Quebec, will also be raised to 50 kilowatts, and the power of CBR, Vancouver, will go up to 10 kilowatts. These power increases will
iMr. McCann.]
improve the service to listeners, particularly in parts of these regions away from the larger cities. They will also protect for Canada the classification of the frequencies under international agreement. I want to stress that point, because it is very important.
On the union of Newfoundland with Canada we made provision for the CBC to take over the facilities of the broadcasting corporation of Newfoundland, and to incorporate them into the national system of Canada. Line connections between the two systems previously had not existed; but by strenuous efforts of engineers of the Canadian National Telegraphs, the Department of Transport, the CBC and other co-operating authorities, a permanent connection was established just in time for the day of union which, as we heard in this house, was exactly one year ago this midnight. I think the house will agree that this was an important development for the greater Canada. The first day of the new confederation last year people in Ottawa and all parts of Canada were able to hear the ceremony at St. John's, and listeners in Newfoundland as well as other parts of the country heard the ceremony on parliament hill. Since then listeners in Newfoundland have been able to hear much of the same broadcasting that goes out to other Canadians, and listeners in other regions have been able to hear voices and reports on the air directly from that new province. Probably no single Newfoundlander, any more than any other listener, likes all the network programs he can hear, but I think the national radio system has helped and can still help much further in promoting mutual knowledge and understanding between the new province and the other regions of Canada.
The committee will have before it the annual report of the corporation. The report speaks bluntly of the basic financial position of the system, and of the danger of having to reduce services severely unless the revenue basis is changed. The fundamental difficulty seems to arise from the fact that because of the general increase in price levels during the last twelve years cost rates to the corporation have risen greatly, while at the same time its main revenue rates have remained unchanged. The corporation faces a number of demands from different parts of the country for new or improved services. It reports that it will not be able to meet these demands, and will in fact have to cut its services drastically unless its revenue basis is changed. The committee will undoubtedly wish to examine the finances of the corporation. It may wish to consider questions of present expenditures and revenues. It may wish to consider the basic situation of the corporation looking to the years ahead, though it may

wish to leave basic financial questions until the report of the royal commission now sitting under the chairmanship of the Right Hon. Vincent Massey is received.
The royal commission is making an extensive study of broadcasting questions. It has held hearings now at many points in nine provinces. I understand that it will have a further series of hearings in Ottawa in April which, with a following visit to Newfoundland, will likely complete its public sittings. I understand we may expect the report in a few months; and I believe this report will be of great value in view of the wide study made by the commission not only of the national system but of other broadcasting activities and of a large number of submissions from the public. This committee may decide to deal with some broadcasting matters which appear of immediate concern, and to leave others for consideration after the report of the royal commission has been made.
Television is one very important aspect of broadcasting that is being studied by the royal commission. In this house a year ago I gave a statement of the interim policy of the government in respect to television pending the report of the royal commission. We thought the time had come to begin the development of television in Canada, and we thought that at the beginning a foundation should be laid to provide for a basic service of Canadian television in the national interest, using Canadian talent and Canadian ideas, and with provision for participation by private enterprise. To this end the policy provided for permission to the C.B.C. to establish production centres in Montreal and Toronto, with associated transmitters, and for the first financing for such development. These centres would be set up to supply a certain service of programs to other stations which might be established in other areas. In view of the high costs of television we suggested that any private groups interested in any area should join their resources to try to provide the best possible operation. So far no such applications have been made. The C.B.C. is going ahead with the production centres in Montreal and Toronto.
No doubt the royal commission will have recommendations to make on the further development of television. The committee may wish to consider present plans. I hope that, in any study of television questions, full consideration will be given to the national needs and interests of Canada as a nation. Television is very far from being just a question of whether certain interests should have the opportunity to set up an operation on one of the few public air channels available. Such an opportunity becomes a monopoly
Radio Broadcasting
position to a large extent, and therefore the question needs careful consideration, with full thought for the future as well as the present. Television as it develops will become a strong social force. That force can be for the good, or the opposite. It can serve to weaken the nationhood of Canada, or to strengthen it. I believe that all studies of these matters should be on the basis of how television can best serve the public in a good sense, and best serve the interests of our Canadian nationhood, under our special Canadian conditions.
As well as carrying on its national service in Canada, the C.B.C., acting as agent for the government, operates the international service broadcasting by shortwave to other countries. This service was started during the war. I can remember members from across the house pressing particularly for its establishment. We thought that it would be also very useful in peacetime in helping the knowledge and understanding of Canada in other countries. Now in a time of "cold war", I think its importance is even greater than we expected it would be. It is very useful, I think, for the service to be able to help keep people in other English-speaking and Latin-American countries informed about Canada; about our attitudes, our activities, and our trading possibilities. But perhaps now it is even more vital to be broadcasting regularly to people of many countries in Europe, where the seeds planted from the east are at work, and where knowledge of how this Canadian democracy works and thinks can be so encouraging. Canada, while not one of the great powers, has a voice that is listened to with respect in many parts of the world. One of the ways in which that voice is heard in a very direct way is through the international service. And where the service goes behind the iron curtain, as it does with the well-established Czech service, I think its value is inestimable.
The service is carried on in close continuous consultation with the Department of External Affairs, and with other departments as appropriate. The responsibilities of the service have always been recognized, and great care taken to carry them out properly and securely. In consultation with the proper government authorities, and with full use of the R.C.M.P., careful measures have been taken over a period of years to make sure of the security and the loyalty of the staff of the service. The measures taken have not been sporadic, but form a continuous process. They started on a general basis in 1946, were made still more detailed in 1948, but are still going on and will continue to go on. I am kept informed of the measures taken, and I believe they provide the fullest possible assurance of a loyal staff. For that reason I regard as

Radio Broadcasting
very unfortunate remarks made outside the house tending to reflect unfairly on members of a staff that have not only shown their integrity by their work and attitudes, but have also been checked very thoroughly by the proper agency, and when a watchful eye is always being kept. Because precautions are taken, it is no reflection on members of a staff. They are merely added safeguards which are necessary these days in such a service.
It is unfortunate that because the international service is beamed to other countries it cannot be heard easily in many parts of Canada, so that it is difficult for Canadians to know what it is saying daily to other countries. Probably the committee will wish to examine some of the output and activities of the service. I can assure them that if they visit the international service headquarters in Montreal they will find that it is quite fascinating to see and hear the daily work of the service.
I think the committee might also be interested in going to Montreal to see the Radio Canada building, formerly the Ford hotel. It has been partly occupied for some time, and shortly will be fully occupied. We arranged to buy and transform this building to provide headquarters for the international service, which had been housed in several unsatisfactory locations, the main one of which it had notice to vacate. It provided for the consolidation in one building of all C. B. C. operations in Montreal, which had been scattered among different buildings under highly unsatisfactory conditions. The national service of the C. B. C. will pay proper rent for its share of the use of the new building. I think that on seeing the new building the committee will agree that it will provide very satisfactory quarters for the complicated Montreal operations of both national and international service for a decidedly reasonable amount under present-day costs.
Mr. Speaker, the national radio system has a task that is more complicated, difficult and expensive than is realized by many Canadians, and perhaps by many members of the house. It has to try to cover this huge country of ours from the Avalon peninsula to Vancouver island, with all its different regions and time zones. It has to maintain services in two languages. Above all, it has to try to meet the varying tastes and wants of different people. There are plenty of things on the air which I do not like or do not agree with. But I know that probably some other people like them or agree with them. The national system should be completely impartial in trying to meet tastes of different groups in IMr. McCann.]
as fair proportion as possible, and giving different opinions equitable chances to be heard.
I hope that members of the committee, in considering the programs and activities of the corporation, will take a large view. I hope they will consider matters not from narrow viewpoints, but on the basis of the general good and fairness to all opinions, tastes and needs in Canada. And I hope particular objections or criticism will not prevent them from taking pride in an over-all Canadian accomplishment.

speechtext:
think the hon. gentleman has reason for complaint, Mr. Speaker; because, after all, there are twenty-five members on this committee. There are five Progressive Conservatives, two C.C.F., one Social Credit and seventeen Liberals. It seems to me that among the seventeen Liberals one could have been found from Prince Edward Island. I did not rise for the purpose of saying that, however, except to join my plea to that of
Radio Broadcasting
the hon. member and to urge that something be done to meet the lack of representation of Prince Edward Island.
I greatly regret that this year I shall not be on the radio committee. I have been on every one of the radio committees that has been established by this house in the past. I have found great interest in the work and have enjoyed it immensely. It is only because of the pressure of work that I am not able to sit on that committee this year. During the years I have been on the committee I have watched the development of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I remember, as the minister stated in his address just now, that when first of all the commission was set up, followed by the corporation, it was generally agreed among all parties in the house that a national system of broadcasting should be dominant in this country. I think that the corporation has performed a remarkable service to the people of this country in the few short years of its existence. When I have the opportunity to do so, I invariably listen to some of its many good programs. I want to compliment the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on their Wednesday night program. I think those of us who heard the program this week, for example-the music, the songs, the description of Sweden-realize the value of interpreting that country to this one even as our international service of our Canadian Broadcasting Corporation interprets Canada to Sweden and to the other countries.
I think the educational part of the work of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is the phase of it that should be specially noted and specially mentioned. Whenever I get the opportunity I listen in even to "Kindergarten of the Air", a remarkable program. A few days ago a little boy whom I know in this city, while listening to "Kindergarten of the Air", heard the kindergarten teacher who was giving the broadcast say "take your thumb out of your mouth." The little fellow had his finger in his mouth and he pulled it out immediately, so interested and intent was he on the program. Programs that are of educational value we get regularly only through the broadcasting corporation. Once in a while we get perhaps a program over one of the private stations; but the regular programs that are of educational value are heard from day to day and week to week over the C.B.C.
I think too that a great deal of credit is coming to the corporation for the work it has done in raising the standards of appreciation of music and for some of the opera that we have heard by the Canadian cpera singers, young men and women of the conservatory

Radio Broadcasting
of music in Toronto, young men and women who have won various awards in competition, joining together to give Canada the kind of entertainment that we have hitherto been unable to get from our own citizens.
I enjoy the opera which comes from the United States on Saturday afternoons in the winter, but I enjoy much more the opera that comes from the C.B.C. from our own Canadian artists; because I like to think that this country is developing not only in the material but in the cultural way. I think that the broadcasting corporation has done an excellent job in bringing together these young singers, training them and enabling them to give the kind of program that we have heard from time to time, this winter more particularly, as well as last winter.
Then of course I know of the awards that have been given to the broadcasting corporation for some of its programs. Some of the productions on "Stage 50" programs, as well as some of the Wednesday evening programs, compare in artistry and in cultural value with anything that is done elsewhere. I think it is remarkable that the C.B.C., with its limited resources, has been able to retain the services of several outstanding young men and women-I will not mention their names because there are several of them- who have given Canada a fine example of what can be done in the field of drama. Out of this C.B.C. programming in opera and drama, I have hoped that we are getting nearer the day when we shall have in this country a national theatre, with opera, drama and ballet assisted and even subsidized by the state itself. I know that when I meet people who come from some of the small European countries such as Latvia they tell me of the fine opera houses and the fine national drama that they had in the city of Riga. I wonder when we are going to have something similar in our own country, because after all man does not live by bread alone. We need the cultural activities as well.
This evening, just before I came down to the house, I listened to one of the very excellent talks in the series given by Professor Phelps of McGill university, stories of travel, on the interpretation of Britain, England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales and so on. They have been of a very high order and I have, as others have, enjoyed them very much indeed. Another example is commentaries from overseas, commentaries by Matthew Halton and others who speak without any censorship, and who speak as they see it, not always of course acceptable to some because we have men of different views and different types on the air; but none the less giving us a picture of international affairs that is well worth while

from the point of view of the progress and education of the Canadian people. Of course I should not omit to say how valuable the commentaries from the United Nations have been ever since the United Nations was set up. I think these projects should be commended when we have the opportunity to commend them. No private stations, with their dependence on advertising, give us the kind of programs that we are getting from the broadcasting corporation.
I should like to see advertising entirely eliminated from Canadian radio. I know that probably that will not be done now. I noticed, though, the other day that a spokesman for the association of broadcasters, when speaking in New York, suggested that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should do no advertising. Well, I wish that were possible. Perhaps it might be made possible if the government recognized that, if we are to have advertising and the private stations are to do it, something, say 25 per cent or 30 per cent of their gross receipts from advertising, should be handed over to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to enable them to put on the cultural and other programs that they think the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be undertaking. In that way perhaps advertising could be eliminated from the C.B.C., and the others, if they were permitted to do so, could go ahead. If they set aside 30 per cent, we will say, of their gross advertising receipts, a substantial sum would come to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Perhaps they have that in mind, because naturally if they think of cutting out all the advertising from the C.B.C. they must of necessity have some views as to how the money would be raised to carry on the kind of work that the broadcasting corporation must undertake on behalf of Canada.
I want to say that the many activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the forums and the other programs that I have already mentioned, are heartily supported by organizations of our farmers, of our workers, and of our professional people, and so on, because they give to Canada something that we seldom get in any other way, namely, a free and frank discussion of problems that are affecting the people.
I sometimes go to the United States. I was there the other day, and as usual when there I hear comments on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The comments are favourable, indeed laudatory. Again and again I hear the remark that our news service is particularly appreciated on the other side of the line because it is not sponsored. There is no advertising. As a rule the news service is pretty objective in its reporting. Of course

I understand that the broadcasting corporation news room has to rely on the Canadian Press, and on the United Press and other news gathering agencies. But with the agencies that are supplying the news to it, the C.B.C. does the best job it possibly can, and one which I think is pretty objective reporting as a rule-objective, of course, from the news agency in the first place, and secondly, objective when put together by those who write the scripts for the newscasts over the C.B.C.
When the committee is set up I hope it will go into this matter of advertising. Advertising on the radio, and particularly on the private stations, has become a sickening experience. I do not know what kind of people some of these advertising agencies think our people are. These singing commercials that you hear are examples. One would think that they were appealing to a nation of morons. Then the statements that are made with absurdly extravagant claims are obviously ridiculous. You hear one soap company telling you that its product washes clothes whiter. Then a few minutes later you hear another soap company contending that its particular soap contains some ingredient or other that makes the clothes whiter than new, and so on. You know perfectly well that they cannot both be telling the truth, and you know perfectly well that what they say are unmitigated falsehoods.

I also want to say that I have followed with a great deal of interest the criticisms of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by the private stations. The Canadian Association of Broadcasters is, in my opinion, a closely knit combination in this country. I believe that if the Combines Investigation Act were amended, as it should be, to prosecute combinations in the supplying of service, the Canadian Association of Broadcasters would come under the heading of a combine. I happen to have before me the rate sheets of most of the stations in Canada, sent out by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. I have forgotten how many there are, but it is a very large volume. Some of them are originals, some of them are photostatic copies, but they are all alike. Some of the rates for the same power are alike. Some for the same power with different coverage are not alike. You find however that the Canadian Association of Broadcasters has a standard rate for the various stations of Canada. They have their time classification, and their standard rates structure for broadcasting.
The one I have in my hand, picked at random, is for station CFNB, Fredericton. It has class A rates for various periods, including from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m. daily, and class B from 6.30 a.m. to 6 p.m. and 11 p.m. to 12.15 a.m. daily.
I notice one reminder printed in heavy black letters at the bottom-and this will be of interest to members of parliament-is that political broadcasting takes single time class A rates, which is the highest rate of all. It seems to me if we were really the democracy we like to think we are we should be promoting free discussion whenever possible and in every possible way, within reasonable limits of course as to time, at the lowest and not at the highest rates.
I appreciate that private stations do give reports from parliament hill. I am also reminded however that when an election comes round radio time is available in large quantities to those who can purchase it, but it must be purchased at the highest rate.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that at election time the newspapers do exactly the same thing?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
The hon. member says that at election time the newspapers do the same. That is right; I know that is perfectly true.

Radio Broadcasting
But let me point out that, through the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the parliament of Canada alienates to a private station a public utility or channel. The newspaper, of course, is purely a matter of private enterprise in every respect, and on a very different basis.
Radio occupies a public air channel and, as such, it is a public utility and in a different class altogether from newspapers or magazines. So I suggest that when the committee meets it should go into the manner in which private stations are operated, examine their logs once again and see how much, or more likely little, they are doing to develop local talent, see how much they are giving to spot announcements which interrupt programs during most of the day. It should see to it that protection is given to the Canadian public against much of the kind of radio we are getting today.
I wish to criticize the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, too, after I have complimented them on some of the things they have done. When the C.B.C. was established it was never contemplated that the high-power channels granted to this country under the Havana treaty should be alienated to private stations. It was never contemplated that we would have stations privately-owned with power of from 10,000 to 50,000 watts; and it seems to me that over the last few years the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has played into the hands of powerful broadcasting interests in this country, and has alienated valuable channels which should have been retained for the public.
I have read the debates in the house, and I sat on the radio committee for years and know it was never contemplated, perhaps until the last radio committee sat, that these channels reserved for high-powered stations would be turned over for private operation. It was always considered that these would be the property of the people of Canada, and for the use of our publicly-owned radio system.
I regret very much indeed that over the past few years, perhaps in the past ten years, these have increased in power, bit by bit, first from 1,000 to 5,000, then from 5,000 to
10,000	and then from 10,000 to 50,000-all the way up. And bear this in mind, that the high-powered station may be a menace to the local community station. I have no criticism of the local community station that is doing the job some of the local stations are doing. I believe that in any national system of radio broadcasting there should be an opportunity for local community stations. But local community stations do not require 50,000 watts. They do not require 10,000 watts; and they should have been kept within the limits dis-
[Mr. Coldwell.l
cussed in the house years ago of 1,000 or, at the most, 5,000 watts. We have some very good smaller stations across Canada, but these powerful 50,000-watt stations are able to get the advertising and to blanket the countryside over the area that should be served by the community stations.
The minister referred to television. I have noticed, and read with a good deal of regret, that certain private interests have been invited to participate in the establishment of television in this country. I believe television is too dangerous a medium to be placed in commercial hands. I will tell you why: it is because it is going to be a very expensive medium to use; and for that reason only powerful organizations will be able to put together the kind of program and pay for the kind of broadcasting that will have to be done on television.
A couple of years ago I witnessed a demonstration. This was not a demonstration against privately-owned television, but rather one to show what might be done in the field of television. This is what can be done: the presentation on that occasion showed a kitchen in which there was a lady preparing to make a pie. In doing so she took from the shelf a certain brand of flour. Not only did she name the flour and thus advertise it, but the picture was there before the eyes of those who were watching. The same applied to all the other ingredients-right down to the package of eggs to be used. Each ingredient was advertised not only by name but by picture, which is much more potent.
It seems to me that if television is to be used in that way it will be almost impossible for any of the smaller interests, who are producing commodities in competition with those of some of the large business concerns across the country, to survive. Precisely the same applies to the big departmental stores that will be able to advertise their wares by television, while the smaller merchants in the same area will find the competition from those larger stores almost impossible.
I say advertising should be kept off television waves altogether, that it must be entirely in the hands of an independent government organization-and when I say "independent", I mean independent of the day-today control of the government of that day. It must be used as a public educational facility. That is going to be costly; and if we are going to have that kind of television, which I suggest is the only kind we can safely have, then I think we shall have to find in some way the ways and means of financing it from the public treasury. I know it is impossible to get people to agree to an increase in the radio licence fee, but I think we must see to it that the corporation is adequately

financed. Speaking personally, I think the radio in my home is worth, not $2.50 a year but many times that amount because of the real pleasure it gives to some one permanently shut in. But of course all people do not look at it that way. Not all can afford any more than the present moderate licence fee. Therefore we have to look for other ways and means of financing the organization.
If advertising is to be discontinued and if the private stations are to take over and have a monopoly of advertising as they apparently demand, then I suggest that they should give thirty per cent, we will say, or more of their gross receipts from advertising for the upkeep of the national radio system and as payment for the use of a very valuable channel granted to them and over which they have a monopoly.
I do not want to detain the house because there are others who wish to speak on this matter, but I do want to say that over the years I think the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has performed a worth-while service for this country, from the point of view both of amusement and of education. It has raised our appreciation of music and it has brought to us drama such as we never had the opportunity of hearing, not only in our homes but in many of the smaller communities across the country.
I hope the committee to be appointed will go into the affairs of the corporation very thoroughly and will produce a report that will give the broadcasting corporation encouragement, that will help to put it on a better financial footing, and that will enable it to serve the people of Canada even better than it has since it was first established.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy this evening to add my voice to this debate and make some suggestions which I believe are valuable and which may prove of assistance to the committee being set up as it progresses with its work. The other day I was talking with a gentleman about Canadian radio policy and he abhorred the fact that a committee was to be set up at this time. It may surprise you when I tell you that this gentleman is connected with independent radio in Canada. He said to me, "Do you think it is fair to the Massey commission who are sitting to consider this very thing to have a committee of parliament set up now? Would it not be more fair for parliament to wait until the Massey commission has reported and then on the basis of that report let the committee proceed, along with the other work it is expected to do, and bring in its conclusions and recommendations?"
I replied that there had not been a radio committee for the last two or three sessions of
Radio Broadcasting
parliament and that there had been pressure from different sources, quite often from members of the house, that as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a government corporation-there might be some legal technicality as to whether it is a crown company, but as far as I am concerned it is to all intents and purposes-it was about time that it came under the review of parliament. Then I told this gentleman that the terms of reference of the Massey commission were much broader than the terms of reference of this committee, that the Massey commission were dealing with the arts and sciences.

speechtext: The other day the question came up as to whether the house should discuss the proceedings which were taking place before the royal commission and I ruled at that time that the proceedings of that royal commission and the evidence given before it should not be discussed in this house.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Thank you. May I point out that I am not discussing the proceedings of the Massey commission; I am simply stating; that that commission is doing a job and that the terms of reference of the commission are broader than the terms of reference of the committee. I was simply stating that as an answer to the criticism from a radio man of the setting up of this committee.
I told him that even though certain evidence had been given before the commission it was not likely that when the same people gave evidence before the committee they would change it. I said that in all probability any briefs submitted would be along the same lines. Another point comes to my mind more forcibly since you have raised the point of order. I do hope that anything presented to the radio committee will not be ruled out of order because the commission is sitting.
Overlapping between the two bodies cannot be avoided. I believe the minister should give us assurance that this committee will be completely free to discuss radio policy, no matter whether that policy is before the commission or not. As I said, in all probability any briefs submitted to the committee would be the same in content as those submitted to the commission; but the appraisal of the evidence and the conclusions drawn might differ from any conclusions or recommendations that might be made by the commission itself. So I do not believe this committee should be set up if its hands are going to be tied. That puts the matter in a nutshell as far as I am concerned.
There is another matter I should like to state, since I feel rather keenly about it. We in this corner of the house, and I in particular as a member of other radio committees, have been accused at times of being opposed to the
55946-94J

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This is not so. I go a long way with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in what he said tonight. We in this corner of the house want to state emphatically that we think the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have done a good job in many respects. I would compliment them on their efforts to keep the air clean. They have been able to avoid the sensationalism which sometimes characterizes United States radio, and they are to be complimented on that. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to Canadian newscasts as compared with United States newscasts, and said that many Americans had complimented him on our news broadcasts. He indicated the reason was that here there was no advertising. I do not know that this is particularly the reason our United States friends may have been impressed by our newscasts. I do not think they object to an advertising plug in the news as much as they object to the sensationalism that characterizes some of the United States newscasts. Some of their commentators like to dig up a lot of dirt and spill it into the ears of the American people. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are to be complimented on their attempt to keep the air waves of Canada clean. They do not stand for slander and such things; character assassination is not tolerated.

speechtext:
Perhaps it does, largely. I do not know whether it is possible to get commentators who are not at least slightly biased by their own thinking. It does seem to me that somehow or other-and I know I am criticized when I say this-the corporation has gathered unto itself an over-supply of (hat type of mentality. That is just by the

way; I do not have that in my notes, but it is my reply to the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith).
The radio corporation, I believe, have been fair in respect to advertising.- They have not permitted the sort of advertising in which people vie with one another in price cutting, and so on. I believe that is a good feature, and there are many others. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar with respect to the opera program that is sponsored by the C.B.C., though some advertising firms also have done a good deal along even that line. I might refer to the program known as "Singing Stars of Tomorrow". Opera, I know, is not keenly appreciated by a vast majority of the Canadian public. Just the same it is extremely valuable in the cultural life of our country. I am a bit of an opera fan myself; yet I do not understand one word of the Italian language, I am not a musician, I hardly know one note of music, and I play no instrument. Yet gradually over the years I have become quite an opera fiend in a small way. It is a taste that has to be acquired; and when it is cultivated it is surprising how it will grow on one. Whether or not you understand the words, you get the story, you feel the thrill of the music and the singing.
Well, all that is very complimentary to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We are not opposed to it. We are opposed to some of its policies, and we think perhaps radio itself could be made somewhat freer by a revision of the regulations. We have strongly opposed the principle that the corporation should also be in control of radio in Canada. We do not believe that is a good thing. It does not matter whether it is the C.B.C. or any other crown corporation; the same principle would hold. That is our belief, and we have opposed matters along that line.
In the matter of finance, I am not opposed to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation being subsidized. I do believe that, working as they are in the commercial field in competition with independent radio stations, they should be able to operate within the confines of their commercial revenue, plus the approximately $5 million a year they receive from radio licences. I do not believe the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should have to come to the taxpayers for any more money. I may not be an expert at scrutinizing these expenditures, but $5 million is a great deal of money. When that amount is given to the broadcasting corporation, over and above its commercial revenues, I believe that is enough without taking money from the taxpayers.
I should like to say something about the talks department of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am not doing so in an

overcritical fashion. I would say the same thing if huge networks were under the control of independent radio stations. I do not believe the best way for all shades of public opinion to be expressed over the air is through the channel of any centralized authority. It does not make any difference to me whether it is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or whether it is a network brought into existence by independent radio people. Here we have a committee of men set up. The number is not important; it may be a half dozen or it may be more. This committee of men decides that some topic or other is to the fore, so they should have different views about it expressed. The problem arises as to whom they will ask to express those views. They say, "We will ask Mr. So-and-So, Mr. So-and-So, and Mr. So-and-So; they represent different views, so we will ask them to take part in this particular program."
There is a tendency there to centralize within those few men the opportunity-I am not saying they take advantage of it, but I am saying we reach the danger point when we give a few men the opportunity of channelling or moulding the mentality of the Canadian people. I feel quite keenly about the matter because that involves something going out over the air in respect of which the people have no say as to whether or not they want to hear it.
It may be said that the social credit view is sometimes heard over the air by reason of the fact that this party is asked to take part in these broadcasts. I am not concerned about whether or not my party is asked to express its views. My particular point is that John Doe out at Pumpkin Centre may believe he has some wisdom that is of value to the Canadian people. Bias he an opportunity of putting his views before the Canadian people? I know I am perhaps using an extreme illustration. There is no way by which this man can talk to the Canadian people. Nevertheless, he can start in a small way. This is not the function now of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. If John Doe of Pumpkin Centre wants to broadcast some of his wisdom, he can go to the local station, which would be an independent station, and say, "I want to talk on the radio." He would be told that the rate was so much. He has to have the money, of course; I know that. We can say what we like, but one cannot do anything in this country without having the money. One cannot eat without having money. After all, perhaps in Pumpkin Centre the rates for the local station would not be very high.
Many people have started in that way. If what they put over the air has any merit at
Radio Broadcasting
all, it is not long before they are talking over the same station again. If the material has real merit, then the person is speaking over more than one station, or perhaps has a weekly program. Through a natural process that person's ideas take shape and begin to grip the imagination of the people. I believe that is the natural way the thing should develop. Now, I say there is danger in centralizing the authority in the hands of a few. It gives them the opportunity, if they care to take it, of moulding the thinking of the Canadian people.
It is an easy thing to popularize something. As a matter of fact, I suggest that the United Nations organization has been overpopularized. A man almost takes his life in his hands if he says anything against this very august body. Why should that be so? Simply because a mentality has been created among the people that takes it for granted that such an organization is the right thing. Who said it was the right thing? I know I cannot talk about the United Nations tonight, but the United Nations might be a dangerous thing. Because it has been popularized, however, people take it for granted that it is a valuable institution. It might be, but it might also be a dangerous institution. Well, that is the power of radio; that is the power of propaganda. I say to you, therefore, that we do give a tremendous opportunity to a few people by placing the direction of the talks department in their hands.
There are just one or two other things I wish to mention. I should like to say something with respect to the political broadcasts that are given by the various parties in the house. This is not in criticism of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation particularly, but I believe that the formula now contained in what is generally known as the white paper on political broadcasting should be changed. Even though the Liberal party have such a tremendous majority in this house, I do not believe that they should have the lion's share of radio time.
I understand that the three opposition parties here-the Conservatives, the C.C.F. and the Social Credit party-are in agreement on having that time equally divided among the four parties. If the three parties are agreed to that, then there is only one party that is not agreed to it; and that is the party which, in spite of its majority in the house, were elected by a minority vote of the people of Canada. The question is this. Should those who are elected by a minority vote of the people of Canada have the lion's share of the time on the air? As a matter of fact, I proposed this division of time in the radio committee a year or two ago, and I know

Radio Broadcasting
that it might be looked upon as a sort of wildeyed suggestion. But the fact of the matter is that because the Liberal party have such a big majority, they should have the least time.
What are you putting over when you are putting over talks to the people of Canada? Is the objective of those talks to inform the people of Canada? Are you putting over ideas or are you putting over a party? If you are putting over ideas, then the ideas of the smaller groups are just as valuable, as ideas, as any that the Liberal party may have. Some of us over here, of course, think theirs are far more important; but naturally, there is a difference of opinion there. But it is the new idea that should be propounded and should have at least an equal amount of time in comparison with the ideas that supposedly have already arrived. If the Liberal party have already arrived, then the people have had their ideas already. Why talk any more about it? I suggest that it might be as well if a change were made in the formula by which this radio time is divided up among the political parties.
I come now to television. I appreciate what 'the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well) has said with respect to the power of television, that it might be extremely costly and therefore that only wealthy advertisers would be able to use it. I believe, however, at will be proven that television is tremendously overrated. At the present time it is, of course, a novelty. Anyone first looking at and listening to television will, of course, sit there by the hour. But radio has one advantage over television and it is simply this. The housewife can go about her work in the house and listen to the radio; but she cannot go about her work and listen to and look at television at the same time.

Yes, I know; it all depends on who is there. There is just one other matter I wish to mention in connection with television. I am inclined to think that if the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would leave the field open to private broadcasters to develop television side by side with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, television would come to Canada much more quickly than we think. It is on its way; it is developing fast in the United States; and it would come to Canada much faster than most people think. But of course if other channels are not open for development by private concerns, and if the development is to be confined to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, then we may have to wait longer than we otherwise would. I hope that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will not seek to monopolize this field. If they permitted private interests to develop a few channels in Canada, I believe that television would come much faster, that even the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would save a good deal of money and at the same time could still retain the power of regulation as long as radio broadcasting operations were regulated under the C.B.C.
There is one matter in connection with the procedure of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the development of television to which I should like to refer. It has not been mentioned before. I believe the radio committee is entitled to an answer. There

has been some criticism of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation purchasing its television equipment from the United States when, my information is, it could have obtained the same service, and television equipment that is just as good, from Great Britain. I understand that they could have obtained it just as cheaply. Whether I am right in the information I have I do not know, but I believe the corporation will have to give an answer to that question when the committee is set up.
What they have done is to aggravate, shall I say, our dollar difficulties. They could have conserved some exchange in that way. I shall not say anything more at the moment, but when the minister replies I hope he will give us the absolute assurance that the hands of the committee will be entirely free, and that the cry of sub judice will not come up when we attempt, as it may appear for the moment, to encroach upon the work of the commission which is now working on the matter.

No protest is necessary in that regard, because I feel sure that the minister would agree that, regardless of protest, every province should be represented on a committee that is to deal with so important a matter as radio broadcasting throughout Canada.
There are just two matters to which I should like to make brief reference The minister pointed out that this committee should be free to examine the activities of the corporation. Indeed, it should not be stifled in any way. It should be able to secure all information necessary regarding finances and expenditures to be made by this corporation. The corporation comes before parliament from time to time and asks for financial assistance. I feel that so far as crown corporations and emanations of the crown are concerned, which appear before parliament and ask for money, they should be subject to the fullest possible examination.
Only the other day an answer was given to me indicating a course of action that I think is contrary to good parliamentary procedure. On March 27 I asked certain questions in regard to another crown corporation, or emanation of the crown, namely, the Canadian National Railways. I asked: How many Canadian National employees were retired in each of the years with pensions up to $25 a month, $30 a month and so forth? Then I asked whether any of the officials received a bonus, retirement payment or any allowance additional to or along with the regular retirement pension. The answer was that the management had always taken the position that it would not be in the interests of the company or of its personnel to make public information pertaining to the salary arrangements or remuneration paid to officers. That was not what I asked for. I asked, what was the retirement allowance additional to any bonus that was given?

No, Mr. Speaker. I am referring to an answer to a question that I received in the house on March 27-
