-to illustrate my contention that parliament should be furnished with such information. Otherwise parliament is simply in the position of being asked to countenance expenditures, however justifiable or unjustifiable they may be, without having the information upon which to arrive at that decision. I hope that, when this committee is set up, answers such as were given to me on March 27, whereby parliament and I were denied information as to whether retirement bonuses are being granted to officials, will not be given to the members of this committee; for it is a dangerous situation when parliament is asked from time to time to supply money to meet deficits of crown corporations and is not given the right to look into operations such as might be disclosed by a proper answer to a question that is asked, such as the one to which I have made reference.
I come now to the question of television. I do not agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) that television is any longer a novelty. Television has been held back in its development in this country by the policy of the C.B.C. to date, as I see it. Television is receiving consideration in the development of stations to operate it in Montreal and Toronto; but elsewhere in this country nothing is being done in that regard. We in western Canada and British Columbia, and others in the maritime provinces, are asking for television. Certainly if it takes $4 million in money collected from the people of Canada to provide television in only two centres, in the central provinces, then the indications are that if it remains a semimonopoly of the C.B.C. or the. government there will not be that development of television in Canada that we should have.
It is not a novelty today in the United States. Indeed, within the last year the number of privately-owned stations there has increased from 680 to 2,316. Great changes have taken place in technical equipment within the last year and a half, and that answers the objections that were prevalent that it was. impossible to provide television except in areas within 50 miles of a station. Today plans are being made in the United States to connect stations across the continent by coaxial cable and microwave repeater stations. I feel that every encouragement should be given to private industry operating alongside the C.B.C. to develop television in Canada, for if private industry is not given

the opportunity I doubt whether we shall make the advances under this type of broadcasting which characterize portions of the United States where conditions are much the same as they are here.
I believe the experience of the last two years will support the stand taken by the opposition in the committee that, having regard to the disputes which arise from time to time as between the C.B.C. and private corporations, there should be set up in this country a semi-judicial body with powers similar to those of the board of transport commissioners. There is no reason why the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is a competitor of private stations wherever those private stations operate, should be in the position, in the event of a dispute arising over the interpretation of regulations, to demand that such private stations shall submit their case to the competing publicly-owned corporation.
In other words, the C.B.C. is in the position of competitor, judge and jury on matters affecting itself in its relationship with the private corporations. Instances will be brought to the attention of the committee, when it is set up, to establish, from the experience of the last two years, the necessity for the creation of an independent body to adjudicate in respect of disputes that may arise in connection with jurisdiction, or in connection with regulatory disputes as between the C.B.C. and the private broadcasting companies.
In connection with the committee I would make a suggestion to the minister. It is true that the committee has the opportunity of examining the officials of the corporation called before it. I should like to see the briefs these officials intend to present delivered to members of the committee a day or so before the officials of the corporation appear to give their evidence. This would save a lot of time, I am sure the minister will agree that on many occasions we have sat for as long as two or three hours listening to the reading of a brief which, had we seen it in advance, could have been made immediately the subject of examination in respect of those questions in it in which we were particularly interested. We could ourselves have read the brief more expeditiously.
In other words, a brief is merely a guide; it is a submission of all the information available which, in the opinion of the officials of the C.B.C., deserves to be considered by the committee. Why not submit that? Why not let us see it in advance, and thus place

us in a position where we can begin immediately to examine and to do an expeditious job, rather than sit there several days listening to the reading of long screeds which we could read much more carefully and much faster privately.
Originally, and even up to 1938, the understanding was that at no time would the C. B. C. have revenues greater than $500,000 from advertising.

Having changed the policy in regard to advertising, there is justification for the wish expressed by the majority of those who have been consulted in a Gallup poll, that the time has come to do away with the licence fee. Only the other day the president of the private broadcasters made the statement that in his opinion this would be done away with in 1951. What justification he had for that statement, I do not know; but I do feel that when parliament is in a position of having to vote money from time to time-and this is a national venture-the time has come to remove the licence fee for private radios.
There are many other pressing matters with which I might deal, but they can be dealt with when the committee is set up. Let me conclude where I began: let us make this a national committee of the House of Commons. I am making an appeal to the minister: let us give representation everywhere, to the end that from this committee there will come a report that indeed will be representative of all parts of Canada.
I hope, too, that we shall not hear the argument raised that many questions which should
Radio Broadcasting
be dealt with by the committee cannot be dealt with because of the fact that a royal commission is sitting. I am sure the minister will make a statement to that effect; otherwise the committee would be strangled, so far as recommendations are concerned, by the fact that a royal commission is sitting. After all, it is for parliament to determine what is to be done. All a royal commission does is to make recommendations, after hearing the evidence, in order to assist the government of the day and, indirectly, parliament, in arriving at a proper conclusion.
Suggestions have been made that the C.B.C. news service is not always objective. I am not able to speak about the musical end or the drama end of the C.B.C., but as far as the news service is concerned I feel that year in and year out it is fair and reasonable in its objectivity. It could be used as an instrument of propaganda, but while objections will necessarily be raised from time to time I think that the news service, assisted as it is by the Canadian Press and British United Press, is indeed a service of which Canada can be proud.
Reference has been made by people living in border cities to the fact that the news received at intervals over the C.B.C. is up to date and objective and they compare it with the news services in the United States. Those who are engaged in broadcasting the news and preparing it deserve commendation where commendation is indeed earned.
I have heard strong objections to the slanting of news by certain commentators but all I ask is that all sides be represented by commentators on the news or political events.

Every one of us has his own prejudices and is biased on certain matters, and, however consciously we may desire to avoid bias, unconsciously we are affected by it. Everything should be done to assure that in the broadcasting of philosophies all sides should be presented by commentators qualified to discuss the news and comment on events.
This is a committee upon which I have sat during the few years I have been in parliament. It is a committee I look forward to sitting on. A great deal of beneficial evidence is presented to the committee. It is an-educative committee and one that can do a worth-while work in developing higher standards of art within our country and an appreciation of the better things of life.
